Though it can live long under water, it nevertheless draws its breath from the air; whence it sometimes happens that, when it enters a fish-trap - that is, an instrument made of twigs for catching fish - for the sake of plunder, since it will not abandon its prey and cannot return by the way it entered, because the shape of the trap prevents this, and it cannot tear the instrument apart quickly enough, it must in the meantime be suffocated in the water, since it could not recover its breath in the air. Some call this instrument a 'weir.' This beast is so greedy and covetous of food that it gathers the fish it has caught into so great a heap in the den where it hides that, from the excessive stench of corruption arising from the putrid fish, it infects not only its den but even the surrounding air, which some who have wished to catch this beast have experienced, not without danger to themselves. This beast is sometimes tamed by fishermen and skillfully trained to drive fish, by circling around them, into the dangers of the nets, to be caught with its help. Whence it is seen to provide great profit to its masters.

div.head: 67. De locusta quadrupede animali que locusta Iohannis baptiste dicitur.

cit.quote: The locust is a quadruped animal, as James says, dwelling in the regions of the East around the parts of Jerusalem. This animal is quite small, but, as those who have seen it say, it has a large head, fleshy and edible. Whence it is read in the Gospel that John the Baptist ate only the flesh of these animals. Some monks, however, who dwell around the solitudes of the Jordan, as Bishop James relates, say that 'locusta' in those parts is a sweet herb, good to eat, on which John the Baptist indeed fed, not on locust animals. They said the herb was called by the common name 'langusta,' but was properly called 'locusta.'

Augustine, on the contrary, says on this passage that the locusts were animals, not plants. It is more to be believed, then, that Augustine and the Gloss itself, which says this, are right. It should, however, be noted here that the locust-worm and the quadruped locust-animal differ greatly in this: the locust-worm is small, while the animal locust that John used is large, nearly the size of a rabbit.

This animal goes about in swarms; whence Solomon: the locust has no king, and yet it goes forth entirely in troops, which certainly cannot be said of the locust-worm, since locust-worms do not go forth in troops, but move singly.

Aristotle seems to speak of these locusts: for he says that a certain woman raised a locust from the time it was small and young. But when it had grown, she found it pregnant on its own, without a male. In this, then, it seems that the locust is a quadruped animal, and that the female locust sometimes generates by itself, without having a mate.

The mule, as the Book of Properties says, is an animal of outstanding strength in labor, born of the adulterous mixture of the seeds of the ass and the horse. It has these traits of its own: the ass's long ears, a harsh bray, a cross-mark on its shoulders, small feet, and a lean body; but in all else it is like a horse. [Mules and hinnies and animals of this kind, which are generated from different kinds of animals, have no proper species of their own; whence, if left to themselves, they fail to reproduce. But true species, and not otherwise, are those which, if left to themselves, perpetuate their nature.] She-mules can never conceive. Whence it happens that their nature never receives the property of generation from the succession of seed. For it is always necessary, in the procreation of the mule, that the ass and the horse come together. And this is the reason why she-mules cannot conceive: the surplus of the menstrual flow passes with food into nourishment for the bodies of she-mules. But the blood itself, which nature does not need, exits with the surplus of the bladder. There is another reason, too, why she-mules cannot conceive: because the animal is generated against nature, and its nature is divided between the horse, which is of a hot nature, and the she-ass, which is of the utmost coldness. There cannot, then, be in an offspring generated from such diverse and ill-matched natures a harmony of parts and an ordered nature, such that it could generate its like from its own substance, since it is known to have no proper substance of its own kind, although it was generated with the aid of nature from the proper substances of the horse and the ass. [The more a mule drinks as a foal, the larger and stronger it becomes.]

Pliny says: it is certain that from two different kinds a third kind is born, resembling neither parent, and that, once born, it does not reproduce, in every kind of animal. It is recorded in the Roman annals that she-mules have often given birth, but this was taken as a portent. As Pliny says, a mule's tendency to kick is checked by more frequent drinking of wine. From the ass and the mare, mules are bred, and from the she-ass and the horse, hinnies.

The monoceros, as Solinus and Pliny say, is a monster with a horrid bellow, a horse's body, an elephant's feet, a boar's tail, a stag's head. From the middle of its forehead projects a horn of wondrous brightness, four feet long, so sharp that whatever it strikes is easily pierced through by its blow. Once caught, it can be killed, but never tamed.
James says, however, that it never comes alive into man's power, and indeed can be killed, but not captured, because, seeing itself overcome, it casts off its life in a fury.

The mastiff is a beast, as Aldhelm says, quite large, found in many parts of the world. It pursues fierce enemies as if created for this purpose. It has a great and huge gape, strong and prominent teeth, with which it boldly wages war against its adversaries. And though it is terrible and fearsome to strong men, and boldly attacks those who cross its path, it wondrously stands in awe of the innocence and smallness of children, and flees from their blows, and in this the greatness of true innocence is proven.
And it is no wonder, because the fierceness of beasts was created not to destroy innocence, but to punish the harmfulness and malice of men.

The mauricomorion is a beast of the East, as Aristotle says, whose size is that of a lion. It is a most fierce animal, reddish in color. It has three rows of teeth. Its feet are like a lion's, and its hair is like a lion's, but its face, eyes, and ears are like a man's, and its eyes are of a dark color. Its tail is like the tail of a field scorpion, with a little redness in the tail. The sound of its mouth is such that you would think you heard a man speaking, and its voice is like the sound of a trumpet. It runs swiftly like a stag and hunts men, devouring and eating them.

The manticore is a most monstrous animal, as Solinus and Pliny write. It has a face almost like a man's, grey-blue eyes, a blood-red color, a lion's body, a tail armed with a scorpion's sting, and a voice so hissing that it imitates the melodies of pipes and harmonizing trumpets. It craves human flesh most avidly. It is as swift in running as a bird in flight. This beast has a triple row of teeth.

The musk-deer, a beast of the East, as Platearius says, is the size of a roe deer, in whose groin an abscess grows from gathered humors. When this has ripened, the animal strikes it and rubs it against a tree. From this rubbing the abscess is opened, and matter flows out and, gathering there, hardens, and this substance is called musk, which indeed is the most precious and most fragrant of all aromatic substances. All of its flesh, or even its dung, is called musk; but what flows from its abscess is far better. Musk, having lost its scent amid foul odors and latrines, recovers its power there; for it struggles against the stench and so, as it were, revives through this struggle. It is effective against fainting and weakness of the heart, brain, liver, and stomach.

This animal signifies certain frivolous-minded men and great sinners, whose iniquity, gathered specifically like an abscess in the groin of lust through evil habit, represents by its very magnitude the death of eternal damnation for the sinning soul. When such a man has often seen this and felt that divine vengeance presses upon him because of it, he is pierced with compunction and, approaching the tree of Christ's cross, by which we have been saved and freed, weeps and asks for pardon; and at once, through divine mercy, the abscess of his iniquity is dissolved, and from this, worthy fruits of penitence, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, are offered to God as a most worthy fragrance, like musk. And in the fact that musk recovers its lost scent in latrines, it is signified that when a penitent or a contemplative has lost the grace of prayer or contemplation, he ought at once to return to the remembrance of his sins and consider that he has not sufficiently mourned them, and so mourn and weep the more abundantly, until he feels, through his tears, that he has received again his accustomed grace.

The mamonet is an animal, as the Book of Properties says, smaller in body than the ape. It has a dark color on the back, white on the belly. It has a long, hairy tail, and a neck as large as its head, so that when it is tied, it is not tied in the manner used for other beasts, since a noose could not hold it there on the neck; instead it is tied around the belly, so that it cannot escape. This is nearly unique in this animal: that it has a face very closely resembling the human face, black, however, and without hair from the neck up over the forehead; nor is the nose continuous with the mouth as in the ape, but there is a definite space between mouth and nose, as in man. They say there is an implacable hatred between these beasts and apes, and that they often fight one another, but though they do not prevail in strength, they are superior to apes in cunning and boldness in fighting. This beast is born in the regions of the East, but lives in the West too, as if in its own land. They say this beast excels in a tenacious and remarkable memory.

The shrew, as the Gloss says, is an animal forbidden by the Law; though in its youth it is sometimes strong, day by day and year by year, the older it grows, the more pitiable it becomes. At last, compelled by the straits of its misery, it feigns gentleness out of weakness, though by nature it is nevertheless cruel. For when someone approaches it, it suddenly spreads poison. For it is a venomous animal, treacherously hostile to other beasts.

As the Experimentator says, it especially attacks horses and mules, and this a pregnant mare above all; and, in a wondrous way, though it holds no power at all, it fawns with immoderate flattery, and yet, if power were ever given to it, it would at once reveal the cruelty lurking in its heart.

bibl.author: Postille Hugonis de Sancto Caro super Leviticum Hugo de Sancto Caro

cit.quote: This animal signifies hypocrites and malicious men, whose - as a certain wise man says - feeble vices lie waiting, no less ready to dare, once they have the strength for it. This Brother Hugh of the Order of Preachers sets down in his postills on Leviticus.

div.head: 76. De musione vel murilego, qui et ‘cattus’ dicitur

cit.quote: The mouser or house-cat - or 'cattus,' called in Greek as if 'astute' - as James says, sees so sharply that even in the darkest caves it sees mice as if by day, and, as is certain, with its glowing eyes and the brightness of its gaze it overcomes the darkness of night. It is an unclean and hateful animal. It pursues mice and all their kind, and, once caught, first plays with them, then, having toyed with them, eats them. There are also venomous toads, with which they are said to do battle. After the fight, unless they quickly find water to drink, they waste away with thirst. They are also said to fight with serpents, by whose venomous stings, though they are stung again and again, they are nevertheless not killed.

As the Experimentator says, the cat readily grows wild at mating time. It imitates the washing of its face by licking its front paws. Its teeth are like a saw. They fight among themselves most fiercely, and this most often to hold the accustomed boundaries of their hunting territory. They are most easily provoked to play by men; they delight in caresses. They love warm places, whence, out of excessive laziness, they sometimes burn their fur. They have long hairs around the mouth, and, if these are removed, they lose their boldness. They delight in being handled by a man's hand, whence they express, in their own way, the joy of singing. Furriers lie in wait for them, and so it is prudent that they be sheared. They are most impatiently inflamed by lust. When a domestic cat begins to grow wild, its ears are cut off, so that, the ear-openings being exposed, it cannot bear the drops of night dew or rain falling into them, and is thus forced to seek again the shelter of the house's roof. [The cat is so smitten with love for its own likeness that, if it stands over a well and beholds its own shadow in the well's water, in order to enjoy the company of its like, it falls of its own accord from the height into the depths, and thus, deceived by the vanity of the shadow, is drowned as the water closes over it. This happens especially when the female seeks the male and they are more impatiently inflamed with lust, and this especially in younger cats, which, less experienced, do not know the dangers.]
The weasel is called in the Book of Properties as if 'mus longa' [long mouse]; for 'telos' in Greek means 'long' in Latin.

For there are two kinds of weasels, as Isidore says: the larger is called 'ictis'; it is white on the belly, red on the back. This beast is cunning by nature. It carefully nurses its young and moves them often from place to place, lest by chance they be found.

As the Experimentator says, the weasel sleeps very long and very deeply. It dwells in cliffs and caves. When it wishes to fight a serpent, it arms itself with wild rue. Accordingly they are also said to be skilled beyond every art of physicians, so that, if they find their young dead, they revive them by means of a certain herb known naturally to them. It pursues mice and serpents.

On the island of Poroselene, weasels do not cross over, as Pliny says, and if brought there, they die. In Boeotia too, if brought there, they at once flee, and this in that part of Boeotia called Lebadea.
Solinus says, however, that it kills the basilisk, which itself kills men by sight alone, but other land animals by its breath. But the weasels also die together with the basilisk they have killed.

The Book of Kyranides says: weasel cooked in olive oil until fully rendered, and strained through a cloth, the oil is effective against arthritis and stiff sinews, swelling of the feet, and every catarrh and scrofula. Its left testicle, tied around a hen's neck, makes it lay an egg. Its blood, given to an epileptic, cures him.
The gall of the asp is a remedy against the asp; the rest is poison, as Pliny says.
Pope Clement says that it conceives through the mouth ... and gives birth through the ear.
Isidore, on the contrary, says that those who claim the weasel conceives through the mouth and pours forth its offspring through the ear are mistaken.

Mice are little beasts, as the Book of Properties says, greedy for bread and for the things made from grain for human food. Their smell troubles elephants. They are most skillful in seeking out food, and for this they generally avoid no dangers. Though this happens slowly and gradually, still, from their desire for food, they wear away even harder and more solid materials.
As Aristotle says, if a mouse drinks water, it dies; and this because mice are of a very moist nature.

And it should be noted that when Pliny says the Libyan mouse does not drink, this is perhaps not to be understood of every mouse in general. But since it is certain that the mouse urinates, it is probable that the food it eats is turned into urine, just as is certain of certain men, who drank almost nothing, and yet, their food being changed into liquid substance, produced a great deal of urine.

As the great Basil says: in Egyptian Thebes, if the sky pours down heavier rains in summer, soon the whole region is filled with countless mice. A mouse, finding many cheeses in one place, tries them all, and, having found the best, eats that one, and, condemning the worse ones, shows that they are to be set aside. There is no doubt that mice are white in certain regions, and some reddish; but black ones are what the world commonly has.

Mice utter cries at the full moon; at the new moon they are silent, as Pliny says. There is also a certain kind of them, but much larger, which we call 'rats.' These little beasts are so harmful, when inflamed with lust, that if their urine touches a bare part of a man, it makes his flesh rot down to the bone, and the wound it causes can never afterward be closed into a scar.
In these, at the full moon, the liver grows, as Isidore says, just as certain marine animals grow larger - such as shellfish - which likewise shrink again as the moon wanes.

Pliny says that their generation comes about through licking, not through mating, and that they become pregnant by tasting salt. It is well known that a multitude of them arises suddenly and dies away just as suddenly; yet they are never found lifeless. It is also well established that little white stones are often found with their young, but for what reason is uncertain, except that common report has taught that they cannot give birth unless such a stone is present. It is well known that the inhabitants of Troy, as the history of the Greeks records, drove away mice by drying their bellies.
You will kill mice, as Palladius says, if you make bread or cheese mixed with black hellebore, and offer it to them to eat. We say the same of rats.

In the East there are mice, as James says, as large as foxes, which kill animals and, though they do not kill men, trouble them with their bites. In Arabia a great mouse is found, whose front feet are large, the size of a hand's palm, and the hind feet the size of a finger.

The ichneumon is called in Greek a beast, as Isidore says, because by its scent it reveals both wholesome foods and poisonous ones. Of which Dracontius says: the swine-like creature foretells the power of any poison. It is called 'suillus' from its bristles, because it has bristles instead of hair on its body. This beast pursues serpents. When it fights against the asp, it raises its tail, which the asp watches closely as if it were the threatening part; and when the asp directs its power against this, it is, deceived, seized by the beast.

div.head: 80. De onagro qui et asinus silvester

cit.quote: The wild ass is called 'onager.' On the fifteenth day of the month of March, as Isidore says, it brays twelve times in the night, and just as many times in the day, whence it is known that this is the equinox.

Africa has these large and untamed, wandering in the desert. Each male rules over herds of females. Fathers are jealous of male offspring being born, as Solinus says, and cut off their testicles. Guarding against this, the mothers give birth in secret and hide the young. Female wild asses delight in an abundance of lust, and, not keeping to any measure of decency, often become hateful to the males because of this. And we have seen the same among men, wives held in hatred by their husbands, when they were moved too impatiently toward lust. Nor is this a wonder, since the female sex ought to be more modest and chaste, because it is contrary to nature when a hotter female is colder than even the coldest male, as Hippocrates says.

As the Experimentator says, the wild ass, by a natural cunning, when dogs pursue it, releases its fragrant dung toward the dogs, and, while the dogs are distracted by this, mocks them and escapes and flees to safer places. Among all animals it hates the crowding and habitation of men. It cannot bear thirst. It cannot be tamed. It drinks only the clearest water, and not easily any other. Male wild asses, lacking females, when the mating season arrives, climb to the tops of mountains and, burning with desire of lust, draw in the wind through their nostrils and bray violently, so much so that they shake other creatures with the horror of their braying.

The male wild ass is said to be the devil. This creature once contrived, in Babylon, that the sons of royal seed be castrated, and in Egypt that the male children be killed, lest God's people increase. But even now it can be said that the devil does not wish virtuous men to be castrated by chastity, but rather seems to give them testicles for lustful indulgence. The proud and haughty, walking as it were on mountains, burn with desire of lust, and search with their nostrils, as if by a keen scent, for occasions of lechery, to satisfy their concupiscence, and often, with their braying, wound innocent souls.

Vitalis says that in Poland the wild asses are very large and fierce. They have very broad horns, but short and shaggy, small horn-like growths on the head, and long hairs beneath the chin. When pursued by dogs, they draw in water through their nostrils in great quantity, and heat it so much that they drench the pursuing dogs with it as if with boiling liquid.

The wild ass of India is a large and cruel animal. It has, as Aristotle says, the form of an ass, and has a single horn on its forehead for fighting hostile beasts, sharp, exceedingly hard, and long. It has this in the middle of the head, since the middle of the head is the common boundary between the two extremes. This animal has a hoof-sole because of a deficiency in its nature, namely because it lacks a second horn. But its hoof-soles are sharp and exceedingly strong, recovering in themselves the advantage of nature which they lost through the absence of the second horn.

They are, however, of wondrous size, as Aldhelm writes, and of especial strength; and this indeed is evident, since they seem to exult in their strength. For they tear huge rocks from the cliffs, for no other purpose than to test their strength against the mass of the stones.
The onocentaur, as Isidore and Aldhelm say, is a monstrous animal, of a doubled nature. For it has a head like an ass's, but a body like a man's.
[a variant tradition holds] that the onocentaur has a horse's body, but the upper part human.

It has a face bristling with hair, and hands shaped and fit for every action. Onocentaurs are bristly on the head, and, as it were, begin to speak when they utter a sound, but their unaccustomed lips cannot form human speech. The philosopher Aldhelm says that this monster was not created thus from the beginning of creation among the other beasts, but that, wherever and whenever it has been seen in some part of the world, it is born from the adulterous mixture of man and bull, or man and horse.

But very many contradict this opinion. The blessed Anthony saw this monstrous animal in the desert, as he journeyed to seek out the glorious Paul the first hermit, as the blessed Jerome writes; but he says it is uncertain whether the devil fashioned this, or whether nature created it.
Many, however, say that this monstrous animal exists in the regions of the East, and was created naturally, like many other monsters, for the fitting and due wonder of the Creator.
Against those who pursue it, as the Experimentator says, it hurls sticks or stones.

'Orix' in the nominative, 'origen' in the accusative, is a beast the size of a she-goat. It resembles the billy-goat in part, and has a tuft of hair beneath its chin. It dwells in the wilderness, and there is caught in snares. Whence Isaiah, in chapter 51, says: like an oryx caught in a net, full of the indignation of the Lord - understood of the children of Israel when they sinned; for then they were given into the hands of their enemies. It signifies those who, dwelling in the vast and arid desert of this world, empty of all good fruit, are ensnared and bound by the ropes of sins and cast into outer darkness.

This, as Pliny says, is a wild beast of the African deserts, which, alone almost among all animals, is clothed with its fur running the wrong way and rough, turned toward the head. In this it signifies the miserly and the greedy, who keep their surplus not to sustain their passing life, but to satisfy the desire of their heart, which is never satisfied. The miser will not be filled with money. Why? Because the desire is in the heart. But riches, as they are gathered, cannot enter the heart, but are stored away in purses. Hunger, then, is not diminished, but increased, just as the body's hunger is not diminished but grows more ardent when food is seen by the eyes but not brought to the mouth.

This beast indeed is born in that part of Africa which lacks water. For this reason it happens that this beast burns with perpetual thirst. But the robbers of Getulia, that is, of a land which lacks water, have shown by the most certain experiments a marvelous remedy for thirst: that a man endures thirst by this aid, that he use, in a small measure, that most wholesome liquid poured from the bladders of these beasts. This beast, as the Egyptians relate, at the rising of the star called the Dog Star, is naturally seen to dance for joy, its very frame visibly sensing that the rain and cold have gone and the fiery vapors of the sun are at hand, so that the earth may be clothed with flowers and begin to show forth sweet fruits and grasses. No one doubts that at the rising of the Dog Star the heat of summer is at hand, and so the beast rejoices. It is also intolerant of cold, so that it cannot easily bear cold and snow. What, then, could I fittingly say this most wholesome liquid, this water we have spoken of, signifies, except the most rich poverty of Christ Jesus? Which is understood through water for this reason, that it is abundant, and so rich, yet water because it is also the drink of the poor: rich, then, is the poverty of Christ, of which, when anyone has drunk with the worthiest reflection, the most burning thirst of avarice will wholly cease in him, so that there will be in him a fountain of sufficiency, which is from God, leaping up (of water) into eternal life. For what mind, continually reflecting on the poverty of Christ, will not at once, in imitation of it, scorn whatever the world contains, and, having tasted its sweetness, glory in God alone and wish for nothing more? And in the fact that it rejoices at the rising of the star, when calm weather comes and the cold flees, it signifies that the ancient saints, who lived as it were under a time of cold, rejoiced, seeing in spirit that a star - the Virgin Mary - would rise from Jacob, so that from her a man might arise in Israel, who, as the future Sun of Justice, would enkindle with the warmth of grace every man coming into this world. Whence the Lord: Abraham rejoiced to see my day; and he saw it, and was glad.

The giraffe is an animal wondrous beyond measure, to which nature has given a beauty and splendor of color surpassing all other beasts. In its front part it is very tall and towering, so that, with its head extended, it can reach a height of twenty cubits. In its hind part, however, it is low like a stag's: it has a stag's feet and tail, an extended neck, and a horse's head, though of smaller form; but its hide is so variously marked with every kind of color that man would try in vain to imitate its natural beauty by art. Nor does it seem unaware of its own beauty; indeed, when it sees men standing around it, it turns and twists itself in every direction, so as to draw the gaze of all in admiration of itself. This animal, in our own time, was sent to Frederick, the Roman Emperor, by the Sultan, king of the Babylonians.

The sheep, as James says, is a most gentle and most patient beast: it has nothing monstrous in it. Everything in it is noted as useful: its wool, its skin, its flesh, its milk, its digestive products, and even the dung on which it rests. When a sheep sees a sick companion lying exhausted and not eating in the heat of the sun, it is said, though healthy itself, to stand upright against the heat and make shade for the sick one, so that, refreshed, she may rise again to graze.
A white lamb cries 'ba,' and a black lamb cries 'me.' If it alternates 'ba' and 'me,' its color too is mixed.

It is the lamb's nature that, as soon as born, it recognizes its mother among the other sheep by her bleat; and the mother recognizes the lamb when she smells it at the tail, and admits it to her udder. The shepherd errs, as Ambrose says, in distinguishing the sheep, but the little lamb never errs in recognizing its mother. The shepherd is often deceived, but the ewe is never deceived by her natural affection. The scent is the same for all, and yet nature has her own domestic scent, which the dear offspring seems to recognize by a certain special property. Nature has her own uses and domestic senses.

As Aristotle says, shepherds take a sign of which sheep can endure the winter: they throw icy water on their tails; the ewe that shakes it off is strong, but the one that does not shake it off is weak. In sheep there is a greater lack of understanding than in other quadrupeds.
A sick sheep easily infects the others, and for this reason it should be cast out or separated from the rest.

There are four kinds of sheep: some that cannot go far to pasture, and need gardens and streams nearby; some also that are pregnant and heavy, which need a careful shepherd, who, according to Isaiah, carries the pregnant ones, lest they be burdened on the way. Some too are wandering and prone to stray, which need a shepherd who will correct them with his staff or hand and bring them back to the flock. Some too are fat and strong, which need a shepherd who sees to it that they never lack wholesome pasture, lest they weaken and die.
Isidore says that the ram has a worm in its head, roused by whose itching they butt one another, and, fighting, strike with great force.

As the Experimentator says - the ram, or sometimes, though rarely, the ewe - has horns curved round like a circle, with which it strives to defend the flock. Its flesh is harder to digest than that of the ewe. They are hotter, and of less moisture. From natural fierceness it strikes the ground with its right foot (when it is angry, or startled, or afraid), and this especially in mating season. For half the year it lies on one side, and for half on the other [in winter, however, on the left, since that side is colder]. 'Agnus' [lamb] is so called from 'recognizing its mother' [agnoscendo matrem]. Lamb's flesh is difficult of digestion, yet easily leaves the stomach, though it is loosed from the limbs with great difficulty, whence it generates a viscous humor. A yearling lamb - that is, of one year - is more praiseworthy because of its temperate balance of moisture and dryness.
And indeed, though Galen says that cheese is generally bad, yet Pliny says that Zoroaster lived twenty years in the desert on cheese alone, so well-tempered that he felt no pain of any disease.

It must indeed be distinguished, when cheese is generally called very bad. There are three things in milk: namely whey, butter, and cheese. Whey is good, butter better; but cheese by itself is worst. It should be noted, then, that cheese which is close to the milk, and rich and buttery, is both good and healthy for the healthy.

Cheese pressed too little becomes riddled with holes, the moisture forming little cavities. You can give it whatever flavor you wish, by adding whatever seasoning you choose, whether pepper or some other spice, sprinkled as powders into the rennet.
A lamb, dreading a wolf though it has never seen one, flees at once, whereas, seeing a horse or another animal, it would neither flee nor be afraid.

Many prefer winter lambs to spring lambs, and this animal alone is usefully born in winter. It is natural for the ram to disdain young ewes and prefer more mature ones; old age is useful to the ram. Its ferocity is checked by piercing its horn near the ear. With the right testicle bound (or removed), it begets females; with the left, males. Thunder causes solitary ewes to miscarry; but the remedy against thunder is to gather them together in flocks. By a north wind they conceive males, by a south wind, females.

[continuation:] they conceive. [Cheese pressed too little becomes riddled with holes, the moisture forming little cavities. You can give it whatever flavor you wish, by adding whatever seasoning you choose, whether pepper or some other spice, sprinkled as powders into the rennet.]

As Palladius says - that eminent authority on the cultivation of vineyards and seed-crops - rams of the whitest color should be chosen, with soft and curling wool, whose tongue should be examined. If it is spotted, it produces variety of color in the offspring. From a white ram, offspring of another color is often born; from dark rams, a white one can never be produced.

In some lands sheep generally bear two young at once; in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Italy sheep bear young twice in one year, whence it can be said of them, quite literally, what is said in the Song of Songs: all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren.

In a sheep, good breeding is marked by the shortness of the legs and the covering of the belly. For those with bare bellies were condemned as 'apriscae.' But those which are most woolly at the tail are known to be of notable quality. Their wool is judged excellent by the fineness and curling crimp and density of the fleece.

Sheep are fattened by drinking much water, and this more so after midday, if they have drunk muddy water; whence some shepherds are accustomed to give them salt in their food, so that they drink more; and through this they give more milk (Aristotle). Sheep become barren through excessive fat. Sheep, above all other quadrupeds, give milk for a long time, namely for eight months. The milk of black sheep is more abundant and better; but the opposite holds for goats: for the milk of white goats is better than that of black goats. If sheep or goats conceive in a place facing the blast of the north wind, males are born, and facing south, females; and they should have their faces turned either to the north or to the south. Accordingly, if the veins beneath its tongue are white, it will bear a white offspring; if black, a black one; if of two colors, likewise of two colors; if red, a red one.

The ewe, as winter approaches, seizes grass with an insatiable, unappeasable hunger, as Ambrose says, because she senses beforehand that a harsh winter is to come, so that she may fill herself with grass before all vegetation fails under the burning frost.

Sheep led to pasture in dry places live longer; but in marshy places, if they graze there often, they become sickly and cannot live long. The life of sheep is ten years, or at most twelve. Sheep bear young up to eight years, and, if well cared for, up to eleven. It is said that they die soon after May, or in the month of May itself, if a honeyed dew falls on the grass at night; and also in the month of August, if they eat dry ears of grain to satiety and afterward drink, they at once die, their innards burst. They often crop grass down to the roots, but if they graze on trees, the trees will scarcely ever thrive. Its bite is deadly to many trees. A sheep can scarcely be driven from a burning house; and indeed if driven out, unless held by force, it runs back to the fire. Sheep of good breed are those that recognize their own shepherd among others and flee thieves. For it is certain that some can distinguish their own shepherd from others. The dung of sheep is judged best of all animals. Everything in the sheep is useful and serves human purposes. If sheep drink water from wells containing salt water, they mate earlier. But if young ewes hasten to mate, it is a very bad sign and a sign of plague among them. Shepherds teach their sheep to walk swiftly at the sound of a certain call. Accordingly, if it happens that a single pregnant ewe remains alone and hears thunder, she will suddenly miscarry. In many parts of the world sheep bear young twice, and this especially in Ethiopia. A ewe can conceive up to nine years of age. But if an old ewe seeks mating after the due time, it is a bad sign.

What, then, does a woman seek in returning to the secrets of the marriage bed after the time of conception? Though this is not forbidden by divine law, nature nevertheless seems, even in animals themselves, to shun it as unlawful. We have said above that this is a bad sign in the ewe, and we find it has also portended evil in women, since those who had lived peacefully before grew foolish through repeated mating.

Panthers [pardi], as James says, are beasts of a kind distinct from the true panther [panthera], marked with a variety of spots. From their adulterous matings with lionesses, degenerate offspring are produced, and lions are indeed begotten from them, but ignoble ones.

Solinus: in Africa, because of the scarcity of water, various wild beasts gather together at the rivers, where lionesses mate with various beasts, either by force or by desire; and from this pardi are said to be produced.
The pardus pursues its prey by leaping rather than by running, and is exceedingly headlong for blood. It often happens, then, that by its violent leap it rushes to its own death.
As the great Basil says, the pardus is fierce and exceedingly sharp in its onset, and has a body matching the movements of its spirit, that is, varied in color.
In that same Africa there are pardi which, hidden among the branches of a dense tree, leap down upon passing creatures and, as Pliny says, prey upon the slaughter of birds.
[a fragmentary note:] cherubim, that is, of the fullness of knowledge

The true panther, as Solinus says, is an animal of varied color, exceedingly beautiful, painted over with small circles, so that it shines with eye-like rings of tawny hue, its variety marked out in blue-grey or white.

This animal is, moreover, quite gentle. It has only one enemy, the dragon. When it has eaten and is sated with various foods, it withdraws, as the Physiologus says, into its den and sleeps. Then, rising after three days, it gives out a roar from its sleep. And when the other beasts hear its voice, they gather and follow the sweetness of the scent that comes from its mouth, but are terrified by the grimness of its head. For this reason, keeping its head hidden, it seizes those it has lured in by the rest of its sweetness. Some relate that on its shoulder there is a mark like the moon, which sometimes grows round, and varies with the phases of the moon. The dragon alone, when it hears its voice, shrinks with fear and hides itself in caverns of the earth.

This beast, as Isidore says, gives birth only once. For its young, not awaiting the proper hour of their due time, tear at the womb with their claws, whence they leave the mother half-dead and useless.
For, as Pliny says, animals with sharp claws often cannot give birth easily; for they are injured internally by the cubs moving within them.

The true panther, ferocious in its excessive swiftness, kills the aurochs, which is the largest and strongest of beasts. For, leaping onto its back, it tears it apart with its claws and gorges itself on its flesh.

The pirander, as Solinus says, is a beast the size of an ox, with branching horns, a stag's head, a boar's tracks, a bear's color, and shaggy, thick fur. They affirm that out of fear it changes its color in various ways, so that when it hides in some place, whether against a white rock or green thickets, it changes to match their likeness. From this it happens that it can be caught only with difficulty.

Pegasus, as Pliny says, is a great and terrible animal in Ethiopia. It has the form of a horse, wings like an eagle's but much larger, a head armed with horns and so monstrous that it terrifies nearly all living creatures by its appearance alone. With its heavy body, aided by the wondrous rowing motion of its wings, they run rather than fly, and, beating the air with the power of their feathers, drive the winds like a whirlwind. They devour much food, move about restlessly, and are hostile to animals, and this especially to man.
The 'hairy one' [pilosus] is an animal, as the Gloss on Isaiah says, which in human form begins above, but below ends in the feet of a beast.

The blessed Jerome, in the Life of the blessed Paul the first hermit, describes this beast as one that is a man above, having a rough forehead with horns, and ending below in the feet of goats; such creatures are called satyrs, or fauns, or incubi. He affirms, and says no one should doubt it, that this monster was captured in the East and seen in Alexandria, and afterward, dead and preserved with salt so that it would not decay from the heat, was carried to Constantinople, so that it might be seen by the Emperor.

In our own age a beast the size of a dog was brought to the King of France: its head did not differ much from a dog's head, but the rest of its bodily limbs were entirely like a man's, its legs bare like a man's, and its hands or arms, its neck white and bare. It had hair on its back. It drank wine most gladly, and ate meat, and this cooked. It took its food in its hands and brought it to its mouth so fittingly and modestly that no one could doubt that in this it had a human manner. It stood upright like a man, sat like a man, and joined most gladly with girls and women, and had the distinction of male and female sex. Its genital member was large, beyond what the size of its body would require. Thus, when roused to fury, this animal moved most savagely, and raged against men. But when calm, it conducted itself most gently and fittingly, like a man, and was soothed by being spoken to, and laughed along with those who played with it.

Baboons are animals around Caesarea in Cappadocia, only a little larger than foxes, which, gathered together like wolves, howl in unison: one starting, and the rest joining in the cry. They have shaggy pelts. Wherever a carcass has been killed, they at once gather there, howling. They also enter tombs and, in hunger, feed on human corpses. Their voice is heard from a great distance, and when it seems to be nearby, their howling is actually far off.

The pathio is an animal which nature seems to have created in the world for wonder and admiration. Its body is colored as if with red blood, and shines in a wondrous way when exposed to the sun's rays. And it is marvelous that, while this brightness is seen in the living beast, once the beast is dead its beauty is soon much diminished, as if it were unworthy for a dead thing to possess such splendor of power. Yet the dead creature's inborn beauty is not entirely taken away, since the redness remains quite beautifully in the skin. This beast's bones are very strong and hard; and its sinews so tough and strong that, unless great force is applied to them, they do not easily break. Some believe this to be the same beast whose kind certain western pagans worship almost as gods. For such pagans are said to raise beasts of this red color, and give them the most delicate food to eat, and worship them, and keep them captive in chambers, and guard them with the utmost effort, lest they ever be carried outside their land; and a capital law has been established for this. They are, however, the size of dogs.

The polecat, as the Book of Properties says, is a beast named from its 'stench,' because it smells exceedingly foul, and this especially when angered. Like the badger, it too has shorter legs on the left side and longer on the right. It dwells in the high and hidden parts of houses. It is most eager for hens and their chicks, since it lives only on flesh and the like. When it seizes a hen or chick, it goes first for the head, so that, once this is overcome, it will not be difficult to work on the other limbs, and so that it cannot cry out while being caught.

The pirolus [titmouse-like creature], as the Book of Properties says, is a beast larger but not longer than the weasel. Its body is red, and white on the belly. It thrives with wondrous agility and is restlessly active. It dwells in trees and rears its young there. It moves from tree to tree more by leaping than by flying, though it sometimes uses its tail in place of wings. For it has a bushy tail, nearly as large as its own body, which it uses for lift in leaping. It lives on nuts and food that is sweet, which it prefers. In summer it gathers provisions on which to live in winter. This little beast, if it must cross waters for the sake of finding food in another region, piles up a rather light piece of wood on the water, and, sitting upon it as if it were a ship's sail, raises its tail on high, and, with a favorable wind blowing, sailing by the effort of its tail, is carried across on the wood.

The reindeer is an animal of the kind of stags or fallow deer, dwelling in Norway. It is large of body and of the greatest strength, most swift in flight. It has its name 'rangiver' from the fact, as if 'bearing branches.' For it bears on its head three sets of horns like little branches. It has two horns larger than the rest, in the place where a stag has its horns, but larger and longer, indeed five cubits long, its branches sometimes growing to as many as twenty-five. It has two other horns set straight in the middle of the head, and these are nearly like a fallow deer's horns, though broad, with many small branches around them, though short. But it also has two more horns against the forehead, not like the other horns, but rather like the bones that are usually found in the shoulder-blades. Armed with these ranks of horns against its enemies, this beast also increases the glory of wonder among monstrous creatures.

div.head: 96. De simia et de diversis generibus simiarum

cit.quote: The ape, as Isidore says, is a beast covered with thick fur. It has limbs formed in nearly every way like a man's. It is keenly sensitive to the elements: it exults at the new moon, but grows sad at the moon's middle and waning phases. It carries the young it loves before it, on its chest and between its arms, but carries the neglected ones on its neck and back.

But it happens, as the Experimentator says, that when it flees from pursuing hunters, carrying its beloved child between its arms and fleeing burdened, it throws that one down, and carries on its neck, unwillingly, the one it hates; for that one clings firmly to the neck of its fleeing mother. And so it happens that when the mother has lost the one she loved, she begins to love the child she had neglected.
[James - a fragmentary attribution]
And Solinus: they are trainable for every kind of game, and forgetful of ferocity. Being clever, they imitate whatever they see, whence they more easily fall into the hands of hunters.

For where hunters have seen them dwelling (for they dwell in trees or cliffs, as Pliny says), the hunters take men's shoes and go and sit in places where they can be seen from above by the apes in the trees. They put the shoes on their own feet and tie them carefully. At last, taking off these same shoes, they leave them under the tree and go far away.

But when the apes see that the hunters have gone away, they climb down and, as they saw done, put on the shoes and tie them carefully. Soon the hunters run up and catch them, entangled in the deceitful bindings, and lead them away captive. Hunters also do another thing to catch apes, as Pliny says. They take sticky birdlime with them and go and sit in a place where they can be seen by the apes. There, pretending to smear their own eyes, they leave the birdlime under the tree and go far away. And the apes, climbing down there, smear their eyes with the sticky birdlime. Then the hunters run up and catch the apes, now blinded.

Solinus: apes are restless in their movements. Beyond other animals, they excel in the sense of taste. They lack a tail, and are fierce in biting; nor are they ever so tame that they are not somewhat wild.

As the Experimentator says, it gladly plays with children and, if given the chance, sometimes strangles them. It gladly eats apples and nuts; but when it finds a bitter rind on them, it throws away the rind along with the nut, refusing the sweet because of the bitter.

bibl.author: Consolatio Philosophie Boethii Boethius Anicius Manlius Severinus

cit.quote: And this is foolish, and contrary to the philosopher Boethius, who says openly in the book of the Consolation: on the threshold of Jupiter there are two jars, one full of wormwood, the other of sweetened honey. Under this condition, then, one must live under Jupiter, that to whomever causes for joy come, causes for sorrow come as well.

And it should be well noted concerning the ape that whoever has injured an ape, it keeps a grudge against him for a long time. The ape, then, imitates not man, but the man who remembers the injuries of his fellow citizens. Forgive, then, and you shall be forgiven. For unless, says the Lord, you forgive men their sins from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.

There are also apes that have tails, which they call 'cercopithecoids.' There are also others, which are quite pleasing in face, bearded, with broad tails, and almost unlike other apes in appearance. This kind, though it can be caught, lives only in Ethiopia. Pliny: the kind of apes has a remarkable affection for their young. Those tamed apes that give birth indoors show their young to everyone, and delight in having them handled.

Aristotle: the ape's face is similar to a man's face in many respects, namely in the nose, ears, and teeth: it has front teeth like a man's, and molars likewise. And on its eyelids there are lashes, short and very fine. And on its chest there are small breasts, and this because it has arms like a man's and hands fit for every action. So, then, though it has such a disposition outwardly resembling man, inwardly it has no disposition in common with man, and this less than any other animal. So too the hypocrite seems outwardly to possess the reason of justice, but inwardly has no sign of virtue, but is filled with all malice and all deceit.

In India there are apes, as Pliny says, that are white over their whole body. The Indians hunt these with skillful effort, and, once caught, tame them, making them fit for every kind of entertainment.
Marmosets, as Isidore says, differ from other apes in almost their whole appearance. For they have, in their face, a long beard and a broad tail.

Almost all beasts have their breasts at the rear, near the kidneys, so that their young, being placed lower, can reach them and have them ready when they wish. But man and the ape have breasts on the chest, because nature gave them hands fit for lifting their young from the ground to the upper chest and fitting the young, by means of the hands, to the breasts. What the ape lacks, compared to the human body, is that it has no navel. The ape's vulva is like a woman's vulva, and the male's member like a dog's member. Its feet and the bending of its legs are like a man's. They have heels on their feet, and for this reason they stand upright like man, and stand and run when they wish, but they can do this only to a limited degree, and this by artifice and constraint upon their nature, for nature made them to be prostrate, facing the ground.
For man alone has his face raised toward the heavens, so that it may be clearly evident that, according to the Apostle, his citizenship ought to be in the heavens.

Tigers, as Solinus says, are beasts marked with spots, shining tawny as if with an undulating black variety. They are of incredible ferocity. They excel in such speed that they are thought to fly, and nothing is so long a distance that they do not cover it in a short time, nor does anything get so far ahead that they do not catch up with it at once. And this is best proven when raiders press after their cubs: unless they have the sea for protection, it is in vain for a man to dare to seize their cubs.

But they are deceived in this way, as Pliny says: for when a raider has stolen the cubs, of which the pregnant mother has borne several, as soon as the mother finds her den empty of cubs, the raider is at once pursued. Soon, as the mother draws near, the raider throws down one of the cubs, with which alone the mother, consoled, carries it back to her usual place; and returning, fiercer than before, when she again presses upon the raider, he yields also a second, or sometimes a third cub, unless in the meantime the raider reaches his ship and her provoked ferocity rages upon the shore.

The blessed Ambrose relates another thing: raiders take glass balls, on which the likenesses of cubs are painted, and, having stolen the cubs, when they see the tigers, the parents of the cubs, closing in behind them, they throw down the painted images. The tigers, thinking by the spinning motion that the images are alive, stop. But at last, crushing the glass images with their paws, they find nothing there. Seeing herself thus deceived, she throws herself with all her strength into pursuit, and, spurred by anger, presses more swiftly upon the fleeing man. Again he delays her pursuit by throwing down an image, yet the mother's diligence is not entirely fooled by the memory of the trick: she turns over the empty image and settles down as if to suckle her young. Thus, deceived by her own devotion, she loses both her vengeance and her offspring. From the name of this animal the river Tigris is named, because it bursts forth with the swiftest current from Mount Caucasus, the highest of all mountains. The region of the Hyrcanians abounds especially in these beasts. The tiger signifies the soul, according to how it is accustomed - swift either toward evil or toward good, according to what is said: In your hands are life and death: choose whichever you wish!

Its cubs are good works, the devil is the raider, the throwing of the ball represents vanity, or the throwing of the mirror a false hope of good. The soul intent on the deception of this vanity loses its good works, and thus the devil's cunning is mocked. It also sometimes happens that the raider gives back one cub to the mother, so that she desists from pursuing the rest. But take heed, simple soul: whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all. So whoever loses one virtue loses them all, because whoever has one has them all.

The bull, as the Book of Properties says, is an animal robust in strength and, among all social beasts, gentle enough, except toward those that are hostile through their rapacity toward others. Gathered together in numbers, they fight most fiercely; but alone, conscious of its cowardice, it easily gives way. When they fight, they hold their tongues out, and do nothing with their teeth, but only with their horns: for there is no fear of their teeth. When they graze on grass, they do not damage the roots, but take only what lies on the surface. Bulls become gentler and fit for every kind of work, especially the yoke, if, once castrated, they are kept from lust. The older they are, the more tender their flesh, if they have been fattened.

Pliny: they say that if bulls turn to the right side in mating, males are born; if to the left, females. Conception is accomplished at a single mounting. They give birth in the tenth month. And the cow's first milk, once curdled, becomes a stone, and this is mixed with water for lac. All females have a finer and sharper voice than the males, except in the kind of cows: for the cow has a coarser voice than the bull.

There is a remarkable devotion among yoke-oxen who are companions, as Isidore says, for one seeks out the other with whom it is accustomed to draw the plough by the neck, and, by frequent lowing, shows its devoted affection if by chance it is missing.

Pliny denies that pregnant cows carry except in the right side of the womb, even when they carry twins. Their strength is at its peak at five years. Frequent washing with warm water is said to make them fat. In bulls, nobility of appearance is shown by a grim brow. When it fights, all its threatening force is in its forefeet. As its anger swells, it shifts its feet alternately and scatters sand, strikes with its horns and tears apart with its head, having a forehead strong for every combat.

The philosopher Alcinous criticized the creation of the bull, because it did not have horns on its shoulders, since then it could strike more forcefully. But he was mistaken, as Aristotle says, since if the origin of the horns were in another limb than the head, it would be a great weight to it and would hinder the actions in which human nature is aided by bulls. This same philosopher Alcinous held that the head was the weaker limb in the bull, and he was wrong, since the head and neck are the stronger part in the bull; and for this reason yokes are bound to them on the head, not on the shoulders as with horses, but on the head, namely so that the head, being stronger than the other limbs, may bear the weight. Its neck, moreover, is made of cartilaginous and strong flesh, and for this reason is somewhat inflexible for bearing the appropriate weight.

As the Experimentator says, the ox has sinews of the heart stronger and harder than other animals; the bull, however, has them stronger still. Beef is dry compared to pork and goat meat, and for this reason it generates thick, turbid, and melancholic blood. It gives much nourishment, however, and greatly strengthens; and this is a worse evil (because it is slowly digested, except with strong wine and garlic). Bulls, if they remain many years in mating, grow very fat. And when excess overtakes them, they die suddenly and do not suffer a long illness before death. We see the same thing in country folk and farmers, who, unused to comforts and accustomed to daily labor, [die suddenly rather than lingering]. The bull gladly drinks clear water. The cow's horns are harder than the male's horns. The offspring a cow bears before ten months does not live, since its hooves will not be complete. When cows are very fertile, men say a rainy season will follow in winter. A bull's horns, if heated, can be bent at will. Gout afflicts cows, and they cannot easily be cured. Another sickness afflicts cows, and the sign of this sickness is a drooping of the ears, and they are not easily healed. And when they have died, if the chest is opened, it appears that corruption of the lung was the cause.
As the great Basil says, a draught of bull's blood is deadly.

So great was the care for oxen among the ancients that it is recorded, as Pliny says, as one of the examples, that a certain man was condemned who had killed his own ox, and was driven into exile as if he had killed his own tenant farmer.

[fragment on] the bull that burns with the goad. The bull's blood does not freeze quickly. But the cow's milk is very thick and does not easily freeze from cold, though its watery part separates from it and the remainder becomes thick; but by fire it thickens further. In the region of Ambardor there are cows of such great size that the one milking them must stand upright on his feet. These give an extraordinary abundance of milk. But the dogs in that region are also large, as are all the animals except the asses. Cows often cannot endure the bull's mating because of the hardness of his member: for it is very cartilaginous and sinewy. Aristotle relates in the book On Animals that a herd-bull, once castrated, later mated once with a cow, and the cow conceived by the bull and gave birth. But he says this was not against the order of nature, because before castration it had seed in its member, which, after castration, being discharged into the female, was well able to generate, but never again afterward, because the passage of seed to the member, in its testicles, was cut off by the removal of the testicles. And it should be noted that menstruation appears in cows and especially in mares, and ceases after four or five months. But this happens rarely except in hot regions, where humors and superfluities more abound in animals. But this menstrual matter is also sometimes expelled through the bladder in the urine; and a cow's urine is very sharp. Every animal has thicker urine after giving birth. When two bulls are in a herd, they fight each other, and the one who wins mates with the cows; and when the victor is weakened by much mating, his rival attacks him and, having defeated him, leaps upon the cows in his place, so as to provoke him to fury. The lifespan of bulls is twenty years. If anyone splits a bull's hide and blows into it and afterward gives it food, it will fatten more quickly.

Ambrose relates that oxen know, when rain is impending, to keep themselves quietly at their stalls. Likewise, when they gather by natural sense that the weather is changing, they look outward, and all together stretch their necks beyond their stalls, as if to show that they wish to go out. A bull's blood does not easily coagulate, and this because of the natural heat of the blood; it does coagulate, but very feebly. The bull's warm blood is a remedy for broken bones. [The gall of oxen, mixed with honey, draws out a splinter, or wood, or iron.]

The bulls, as Solinus says, that are found in India have a dark color, thick and bristling hair, a huge head, and a mouth-gape reaching to the ears. They are swifter than birds, and their hair grows backward, against the grain. They bend their horns with the flexibility they wish, either at will or for fighting, and either lower them or raise them.

Aristotle says they cast their dung behind them to a great distance, whose heat and stench keep dogs and hunters at bay, so that they do not come near. By the hardness they have on their backs, they scorn every weapon. They are of such monstrous ferocity that, once captured, they cast off their lives in rage. There are also, in the East, oxen that have only a single horn. There are others there too, armed with three horns on the forehead; these have hooves that are not cloven at all, but solid, like a horse's.

The tranes is a small animal, like a rabbit, as Pliny says, which, though small of body, is nevertheless strong in spirit and robust in strength, and naturally bold for fighting. Nature has even bestowed on its head, as a sign of this quality and of combat, a kind of helmet, by which the skull and brain are protected; and by this it is also clearly shown that the providence of the creating nature has furnished to each created thing what is fitting and useful for it. This animal is red in color, and handsome for its kind.

The tragelaph is an animal forbidden by the Law. As Isidore says, it has the appearance of a stag in many respects: it has shaggy shoulders like a goat's, and a shaggy chin, with bristling beard. It has a head roughened with branching horns, powerful in strength and weaponry to drive off any adversary and keep itself safe from enemies. They dwell around a certain land called Phasis, and are found nowhere else.

Troglodytes, as Pliny says, are beasts which, unlike all other kinds of quadruped beasts that walk on the earth, graze with their horns lowered and their neck bent sideways. And this is the reason: they have long horns hanging down along the slope of the head and jaws all the way to the ground. For this reason, unlike other beasts, they cannot graze on the ground, their horns being in the way, but must bend their necks sideways to cut the long grass, drawing it in with their mouths, rather than crop it as other animals do.
The mole, as the Book of Properties and the Gloss say, is a small, black, and blind animal.
This creature, as the Gloss says, is engendered from earth that is drenched and muddy, but corrupted. As is fitting, it dwells in the earth; it lives on a diet of worms.

The Book of Properties: sometimes, when the earth dries with thirst, it comes out. But because it is blind, it does not know how to return to the place it came from, and so it often happens that, taken by surprise, it is killed. It does the greatest damage to crops of vegetables and various herbs.

As the Experimentator says, it burrows through the soil and, when crops are drying, eats the roots underground. In hunger it eats earth. Its pelt has much fur and is very soft. It has a most hideous color, whence they call it 'alfalcam.' The mole, burned to powder and sprinkled with egg white on the face, is a remedy against leprosy. The blood of a killed mole, if smeared on a head bald of hair, is said to make the hair grow back.
Of the mole, Aristotle says: all animals, he says, that beget their like have eyes, except the mole, which is deprived of eyes, as far as appears outwardly.

For it does not see at all. Yet if anyone splits the skin that lies over the place of its eyes and examines these places with his hand, he will find a certain blackness, and in the middle of it a pupil and the color and arrangement of eyes, and he will see, upon examination, that the mole's blindness and deprivation of light happen only because of the skin or hide let down over its eyes. And in this very fact the providence and wisdom of the Creator is to be considered, who gave to each creature what is fitting and useful to it. He gave the mole eyes, with which, dwelling in darkness and in the hiding-places of the earth, it would not see even were it made able to bear the light. But he gave it eyes, though fully formed, blind, so as both to satisfy usefulness and not entirely deny it the glory of nature. [a near-duplicate version of the same passage follows in the source]

The mole hears more acutely than any animal, as Pliny says, though buried in earth, so dense and deaf an element; and this is all the more remarkable, since every sound naturally strives upward. When the mole enters in spring, unlike at other times, it does not throw up many mounds, but long passages in the earth, raised at the surface. But where these various passages meet, it throws up a great mound and there takes its pleasure with its young. When, then, a flood comes, the water running through these passages to the mound, the mole is suffocated together with its young.

The mole signifies the covetous man, who gathers what returns to him from plunder on every side. In the midst of these he raises up a heap of houses, where he says: Soul, you have many good things, etc. But when the flood of the tears of the poor comes before God, he is struck by divine vengeance, and it is said to him: Fool! This very night they will demand your soul of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? David answers: They shall be the portion of foxes, the possession of the prince and his heirs: the flesh for worms, the soul for the demon.

The unicorn is indeed a small animal, as Isidore says, in proportion to the strength of its body. It also has short legs in proportion to its size. It is exceedingly fierce, so that it cannot be caught by force by any hunter. It has a boxwood color. It has a horn of four feet in the middle of its forehead, from which not even the elephant, for all its bodily size, is safe. It sharpens this horn against rocks in combat. For often, having a contest with the elephant, it lays it low, wounded in the belly.
The Book of Kyranides says: that horn drives out demons: for it is pierced through, and thus by its sound and presence a demon is put to flight.

It does not fear iron. It stays on high mountains and dwells in the vastest wildernesses. James and Isidore [say] it is caught by this device: a virgin girl is set out in the forest and left alone. The unicorn, coming to her, all its ferocity laid aside, venerates the chaste purity of the maiden's body, and lays its head in the lap of the girl as she opens it to receive it, and thus, lulled to sleep, is caught unarmed by the hunters, and is either killed or displayed as a spectacle in a royal palace.
Pompey, as Pliny says, was the first to display this animal as a spectacle at Rome.

This cruel animal signifies Christ, who, before the Incarnation, raged in heaven, punishing the angels for their pride, and on earth punishing men for disobedience, as with Adam, and for lust, as with the Sodomites, and for gluttony, as with the sons of Israel. With no one daring to oppose him, Isaiah cries out: There is none, he says, who rises up and holds you fast. This creature the Virgin, as it were, captured in the desert of the world's wilderness, when, allured by the incomparable beauty of the chastity of the glorious Virgin Mary, the Son of God entered, as it were, the bosom of her womb; and through her, made man, he took a body, in which, seized by the Jews as by the most cruel hunters, he is killed, and, rising from this and ascending into heaven, is set at the right hand of the Father in the palace of the heavenly kingdom.
The bear is an exceedingly fierce animal, misshapen of limb. Skinned, its limbs are nearly like a man's. Its greatest strength is in its forelegs and its loins. Its head, however, is weak and feeble.

Ambrose: the she-bear, on the thirtieth day from conception, bears an immature offspring, a little larger than mice, as Pliny says; it licks the flesh it brings forth from itself and, warming and shaping the offspring, brings its limbs into form. Sometimes they warm their young held to their chest, so that, warmed by constant lying together, they draw in the animal spirit. Indeed, meanwhile, in the first fourteen days, the mothers fall so deep into sleep that they cannot even be roused by wounds. Soon, coming out into the open daylight, they suffer such intolerance of the light that you would think them wrapped in blindness. And so, in the very offspring, when it is born, no limb appears distinct except the outlines of the claws.
Pliny: bears mate not like other quadrupeds, but like men. Certain seasons arouse their lust.

Solinus: the males hold pregnant she-bears in a certain secluded reverence. Nothing is rarer than to see a she-bear giving birth. If they do not have a den, they build one from a heap of branches and brushwood, in places that are most impenetrable, strewn with soft foliage.

Aristotle: female bears are stronger and bolder than the males, as is the case in the kind of leopards; they are tamed more quickly and are more cunning. They have four teats. The bear indifferently eats flesh and the fruits of the earth or of trees, because of the moisture of its body. It climbs trees either from fear or for food. It breaks olive-presses and eats their fruit, and eats crabs or ants for medicine. It eats flesh because it is food of great strength. Bears rather gulp water with their mouths than drink it in the manner of others.

Cooked bear meat, as Pliny says, seems to increase in size, which is contrary to the nature of all other flesh. It has very little blood, except around the heart. In winter, indeed, they wander little, but in spring they come forth, and yet at that time they are very fat, especially the males. The reason for this is not obvious, especially since in winter they sleep very little.

[Physici -] the bear delays fish, the mole gnats, the salamander [fire]. It is certain, however, that in the bear the elements earth and air mingle and predominate, from which it must recover the renewal of its spirit. Whence, by a certain likeness, in winter, when the air grows denser and rises, it goes under the earth, and this because of the colder air. The bear, indeed, being generated from a burnt humor and thus fierce, is greatly harmed by cold penetrating to its interior because of the excessive openness of its pores.

The bear's breath is so pestilential that no wild beast can bear its contact, and things touched by its breath rot more quickly. It fights not only with stags, but also with wild boars. It fights with bulls and leaps upon their backs, and when the bull wishes to strike it with its horns, the bear holds its horns with its paws and throws down its shoulders, casting the defeated bull to the ground. But it does not easily overcome a bull that has no horns. It walks upright on its hind legs when it wishes, and fights with its forelegs too.

Bears never attack a man unless they have first received a blow from him. Except for wounds and mortal blows, they are said to draw out all other injuries and bruises by licking their paws. For some say the reason for this licking is a certain disease of rage, which seizes it for many hours; and this can well be believed, because it foams at the mouth and is convulsed through its whole body. The Experimentator says, however, that the stronger opinion is the one that says the bear draws out pain by licking. When the bear is caught (nor does it tame at man's will), its eyes are blinded with hot bronze: for while it looks upon the glowing bronze, as if without sensing it, it loses its sight. It can scarcely stand still (motionless), without shifting itself from place to place (restless).
The great Basil says that the bear, often pierced by a mortal wound, uses every device to heal itself, especially a certain herb of drier nature, applying it to stanch its own wounds.

It is caught in this way: hunters, noting a hollow tree in which bees have gathered honeycombs, hang a great heavy mallet by a rope, so that it blocks the opening by which access to the combs is gained, and beneath the tree they fix sharpened stakes in the ground. And when the bear, most eager for honey, finds the mallet hanging in the entrance, it grows angry and strives to throw the hanging thing away. But the mallet, swinging back to its place, strikes the struggling bear again. When this happens repeatedly, and the bear, ever more eager for honey, strives to overcome it, at last, exhausted and beaten down by the mallet's blows, it falls upon the sharp stakes fixed beneath the tree; and thus the watching hunters catch or kill it as it lies fallen.

Pliny: when bears attack wild buffalo, they attack either the horns or the nostrils: the horns, so as to tire the buffalo with their weight; the nostrils, so that the pain is sharper where held. Sometimes bears die from tasting mandrake apples, but they devour ants to recover their health.

Ambrose: the bear, indeed, when gravely wounded and afflicted with injuries, knows how to heal itself with an herb whose name, as the Greeks call it, is 'phlomos.' The bear applies its wounds to this herb, so as to be healed by the touch alone, nature showing it the remedy. When endangered by a natural weakness, it devours ants and recovers its health.

The bear, among nearly all land creatures, keeps growing as long as it lives. Whence the largest and strongest bears are found. The world commonly has black bears; but some regions have white ones, and these grow so large that they reach a length of fifteen cubits.

The Book of Kyranides: each part of it makes a medicine for the corresponding part of man. The claws of its right paw, carried, calm fevers. The claws of its left paw drive away demons. Its hide drives away fleas.

The bison [vesontes], as Solinus says, is a beast similar to the ox; it has a bristly neck, a mane like a horse's, and is of such monstrous swiftness that, once captured by men, it can never be tamed or domesticated.

So too certain worldly men, when they come to religious life, are so habituated to the pernicious custom of their crimes that they can never incline their heart to any grace of kindness, but always, fierce and savage, rage against their companions and cast off the bond of Christ's religious yoke. Whence the Lord reproaches such men through the prophet: Of old, he says, you broke the yoke, you tore off the bonds.

The aurochs [urin], as Solinus and James say, is an animal whose horns, like a bull's, grow so large that, once cut off, because of their remarkable capacity, they become vessels for royal drinks borne among royal tables.
Isidore calls these wild oxen in Germany. These beasts are so strong that they can lift trees and armed soldiers on their horns.

This animal signifies those who seek the honors of the world through torments, so that mimics and jesters may seek their livelihood from praising them, as with Arthur. Or it signifies martyrs or saints, for whose powerful merit of virtue praise is offered to Christ, placed as a sacrifice upon the altar.

The uranuscopus is an animal with a broad chest, wide ears, an upright face, a projecting neck, having a single eye at the top of its head, with which it always gazes toward the sky; whence 'uranuscopus,' as Huguccio says, is said to mean a wild ox that gazes upward. This animal excels in cunning above many animals, and this especially in guarding itself. It is notably large in strength and size.
The fox, as Isidore says, is a very cunning animal. It is of quite a reddish color, with a bushy and large tail.

The Experimentator: when a dog pursues it and, having caught up, tries to seize it, the fox drags its bushy tail through the pursuing dog's mouth and thus deceives the dog, until it can reach the thick cover of the woods.

The blessed Ambrose relates that the fox, when death threatens, seeks out the pine tree and takes as food the tear and sap that flows from the pine; and thus it recovers its health and prolongs its lifespan.

During the dog days the fox sometimes grows so gravely weak that it cannot flee; and then it hides in the depths of burrows, naturally aware of its helplessness. For they have burrows in the ground for protection, but they are often caught in these. For hunters, when they know that foxes are hiding in burrows, send in small dogs trained for this purpose, which, penetrating to the top of the burrow where the foxes lie, betray them by barking. And there, digging in from above, the hunters reach the fox lying within and catch it.

The Experimentator says that the fox does not labor in digging its burrows, but a certain beast which we call the badger; for when the badger has dug a burrow in the earth to rest in, the cunning fox unloads its dung at the burrow's entrance, so that, polluted with the stench of putrid excrement, it becomes worthless. And indeed the badger utterly abhors the stench of digested dung, and abandons the place; and so the cunning beast takes possession of it. The Experimentator says that the fox has a foul-smelling mouth, and is foul-smelling also at the rear. It lies in wait especially for domestic animals. [Its gall heals the ears and eyes. Its fat is good for the ears and for gout. Its little pelt, wrapped around a gouty foot with the inner side turned out, heals it. Its liver, roasted and drunk with wine, heals colic. Its heart is effective against flux of blood; likewise its liver. Its brain, given to infants, often frees them from lifelong epilepsy. Its suet or fat is effective against all pains of the limbs. Its spleen too, drunk, relaxes contracted limbs.] If fox flesh is burned, its ash is effective for asthmatics, taken with wine. The fat of its suet greatly helps ear pains. If a fox eats almonds, it is said to die. It suffers a heating of the liver in summertime, whence blood flowing to the surface relieves it, and its skin ulcerates, and through this the hair falls from its body, as Constantine says in the Viaticum.

It hunts the hare, and at first plays with it, then attacks it with its teeth, and unless the hare escapes by speed alone, it is caught by the fox.
