It nests and rears chicks and, when it has nourished its chicks to flight and made them capable, it dies at once and leaves its offspring as imitators of its life and its death, though they too are destined to die in a later season.

The 'echitus' [hedge-sparrow], as Pliny says, is a very small bird, which has an enmity with the ass. For the ass, rubbing itself against thorn-bushes to scratch itself, scatters this bird's nests, which the bird so dreads that, hearing its braying voice, it at once leaps from the nest, and its chicks fall out from fear. But it sometimes takes its revenge. For, flying to it, it pecks at the ass's sores with its beak and does not desist, however much the ass tries to flee.
The gerfalcon, also called girfale, as the Gloss on Leviticus says, in the place where the unclean birds are forbidden, is also called the gyrfalcon.

As the Book of Properties says, it is the noblest of all noble birds. It is of a sky-blue color, though in the greatest part of its body it leans toward white, except on the chest and wings, where it more clearly imitates the color of the sky.
This bird is so strong and large, as the Gloss on Leviticus says, that it overcomes and catches the eagle itself, which is the strongest of birds.
[a fragmentary note listing:] dog, cranes, herodian birds

It does not eat raw or kept flesh, as the Experimentator says, but only fresh. It ascends high and, descending with force, strikes down its prey. In flying at prey it draws its feet up to its chest and thus strikes the prey. If it does not seize its prey on the first strike, it strains upward and, out of indignation, scarcely returns to the lure. When it sees prey, it rouses itself, shaking, and, if it is fit for capture, decides accordingly. There is a certain kind of gyrfalcon called the 'saker,' and these are stronger. They have a dark color.

The phoenix of Arabia, as Solinus, James, Isidore, and Ambrose say, lives alone in the world without a mate, through an age of three hundred and forty years; it is of an eagle's size, with a head adorned like a peacock's, a crested throat, golden brilliance around its neck, and a purple hue. It has a tail of a sky-blue color, in which rose-colored feathers are interwoven with wondrous variety. And when, with the passage of its foreseeing age, it begins to grow heavy, in the highest regions of the East, on a most beautiful tree set above a most pleasant spring, it builds, as it were, a nest-altar from frankincense and myrrh and cinnamon and precious spices. Then, drawing the burning orbs of the sun into itself by the beating of its wings, it throws itself upon the pile, and, the spices set ablaze by the sun's heat, it too is likewise set alight and consumed. Then, after a few days of its burning, a worm, born from the very ash of the phoenix, in a short time puts on the rowing-oars of wings, and then is most perfectly reshaped into the original bird, its mother.

Isidore says: the phoenix bird entered Heliopolis, a city of Egypt, in the month of Adar, that is, April, its wings laden with various spices, and hid the pile of brushwood that had been laid aside as a sacrifice by the priest of the Lord, and burned itself upon the pile, among the spices it had carried on its wings. On the first day after the day of its burning, the priest came and found the wood burnt, which he had placed upon the right altar, and, searching through the ash, found a small worm, giving off a most sweet fragrance. On the second day the little worm was found shaped into a bird. On the third day, restored to its whole and most perfect state, it bade the priest farewell and flew away.

Haimo: it should accordingly be noted that this city, Heliopolis, that is, 'city of the Sun,' was built before the coming of the Savior, in the land of Egypt; and in it, in the likeness of the temple of Jerusalem, in honor of the most high God, a temple was built by Onias (son of that Onias mentioned in the book of Maccabees), by order, namely, of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, according to the prophecy of Isaiah: And there shall be an altar of the Lord in the land of Egypt. In this city, the same Haimo says, the blessed Mary, Mother of God, fleeing from the face of Herod with her son and Joseph her husband, frequently dwelt.

The phoenix of Arabia is a bird living without a mate for three hundred and forty years; it signifies the holy soul, which leads its life simply in the faith of the Holy Trinity and the steadfastness of the four cardinal virtues: prudence, temperance, justice, and fortitude. In its eagle's size is signified the loftiness of holy contemplation; in the beauty of its head, purity of mind; in its crested throat, the twofold affection in prayer for salvation, namely one's own or another's; in its golden neck, the tranquillity of hope, which proceeds from charity; in the purple of its hindmost part, the fulfillment, in mortified flesh, of Christ's passion.

The coot, as Isidore says, is a bird whose flesh tastes like hare's flesh. Dwelling around ponds, it has its nest in the middle of the water, or on rocks surrounded by water. It delights in the depths of the sea. For when it senses a storm coming, it flees and plays in the depths. This bird is said to be understanding and most prudent above all winged creatures. It does not feed on carcasses. It does not stay in various different places or wander about, but keeps itself still in a single place until the end of its life. It gathers its food around itself.

The coot, because with reverent mercy it feeds and nourishes, along with its own young, the eagle's chicks that have been cast from the nest: giving to rational men an example of how much mercy they ought to be moved to show toward strangers, the poor, and the afflicted.

The fatator is a bird dwelling in the regions of the East. This bird, naturally eager to produce offspring, anticipates the season of spring, in which other birds are accustomed to begin their conceiving. Whence it happens that the inheritance rushed to at the outset lacks blessing at the end. For the eggs it lays before springtime, namely while the cold still troubles, are all spoiled through the winter and produce no offspring. But it has a remedy for its comfort: for in the following warm season it mates again and lays eggs; and so these later eggs are brought to completion and produce chicks. This is contrary to almost all wild birds, which mate once a year and lay eggs and rear chicks.

There is also another bird, the 'fetix' - besides the one we mentioned above, the fatator - as Aristotle says, which, though small in body, is nevertheless magnificent in its fruit. For this bird, as Aristotle attests in the book On Animals, breeds twice a year, and its chicks reach their due life and form. And this is because it waits for the due season of summer and does not anticipate the time, as the fatator does, and so, worthy of the gift of offspring, is not frustrated of its fruit.
The fig-pecker is a bird, as Isidore says, taking its name from the fact itself: for it eats figs and grapes, and the sweet fruits of trees.

And it signifies those who, desiring more eagerly the sweet fruits of contemplation, scorn the bitter fruits of death, the sins, of the dragons. Moses, describing these detestable men in Deuteronomy, says: Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter; the gall of dragons, etc. But on the contrary, the bride in the Song of Songs, desiring the good fruit of contemplation, said: And its fruit was sweet to my throat.

div.head: 50. De diversis generibus falconum, sive accipitrum, et de infirmitatibus et medicinis earum. Hic de Aquila, et Symacus, et Theodotion, in Epistula directa ad Tholomeum regem Egipti.

bibl.author: Epistola Aquile, Symmachi et Theodotionis ad Ptolomeum regem Egypti

cit.quote: There are seven kinds of falcons, as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion say, who indeed wrote a letter to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, in which, at his command, they treated of the noble birds we call hunting-birds, according to what they could find in the writings of the ancients. In this same letter it is also written of the medicines for these birds, all of which, for the sake of brevity, we have condensed into a compressed account. There are eight kinds of falcons. The first, called the 'lanner,' of which there are two kinds: one has a thick head and beak, feet like an eagle's, which is trained for hunting only with great labor; but once trained, it is excellent in flight in its second and third year. The other kind of lanner is of smaller stature and is held cheap by men.

The second kind of falcon is called the 'peregrine,' which is easily trained for flight. The third kind is called the 'mountain falcon,' and of this kind is rougher and finer. [The fourth kind is blue-grey in feet and legs, whence it also gets its name; this kind is noble in its first and second year, but in the third year is reckoned most worthless. The fifth kind, slender and long in build, is most excellent in flight.] The sixth kind is called the 'supranicum,' which nearly resembles the eagle, except that in its feet, wings, and eyes it resembles the falcon in coloring. The seventh kind is the British kind, and this holds the primacy among all hunting birds, so that no bird dares to hunt in its presence, nor does any other bird dare to fly while it is flying overhead. This kind has thick feet, knotted legs, cruel claws, a fiery appearance, terrible eyes, a thick head and chest, and large wing-joints. These are also most easily trained for flight and can fly much and long. They wish to be fed most delicately and eat almost as much as eagles. And we believe this kind of bird is the one called above the aeriophylon, or commonly 'aelion': seek, then, its whole nature above, under the letter A, in the chapter On the Aeriophylon. The eighth kind is that called the 'herodius,' or commonly the 'gyrfalcon.' This kind is more common than the aelion kind and is held dearer for the moderation of its food and life. Seek its nature more fully above, under the letter E, in the chapter On the Herodius. The 'tercels' are the smallest of hunting birds, most ready by their nature, on account of their sex, for hunting, and these too are joined to the kind of falcons. There are also four kinds of hawks. The first kind is large in body, very tamable, with variegated, translucent eyes, a thick foot, long claws, a cheerful expression, delicate in eating, delighting in warm-blooded birds. It attacks all birds and fears no eagle. Seek its whole nature, described together, above, under the letter A, among the winged creatures, in the chapter On the Hawk. The second kind of hawk is what we may call the 'osprey'; smaller than the first kind, having thick wings in proportion to its body, short feet and thick claws, large and dark eyes. It does not tame quickly, and so is hateful to many. In the first year of taming it is of little worth, in the second more, and in the third moult it hunts quite well. The third kind of hawk is the 'sparrowhawk,' small indeed in comparison to the others, but nevertheless swift. It tames quickly and wishes to be delicately nourished, and hunts easily. Seek its nature below, under the letter N, in the chapter On the Sparrowhawk. The fourth kind is called the 'frogellus,' which we commonly call the 'merlin.' This is much smaller than the sparrowhawk, but similar in color, just as the sparrowhawk resembles the hawk in its disposition and coloring. It is a bird that tames quickly, is swift in flight, hunts easily, and wishes to be delicately nourished. In its second or third moult it becomes excellent. Having discussed, then, the kinds and natures of noble birds, let us next treat of their habits and medicines, and let us begin with the illnesses of the head. If sickness grows in a bird's eyes, anoint its eyes with olive oil, and this often. If a white film grows on the eye, apply powder of fennel seed and warm woman's milk. If it has grown dim from old age, take a suitable piece of iron, and heat it, and place it over the nostrils, where the crown of the head joins the eye to the nostrils. If it has blocked nostrils, take powder of pepper and stavesacre, and blow it into its nostrils through a small feather-quill, and afterward rub its palate with powder of stavesacre alone. If it has catarrh in the head, place rue near its nostrils, and dip the flesh it eats in the juice of rue. Likewise, put crushed garlic with wine into its nostrils, and let it sit a whole day in a dark place, and let it fast for one day. If it has trouble with the pupil, take its tongue and rub it with powder of stavesacre mixed with honey. Give it butter to eat, if the aforesaid remedies do not work. Powder of dried cabbage is likewise effective. If it is excessively noisy, take a bat, and place ground pepper inside it, and give it to the bird to eat. If you take another bird instead, it will work just as well; for one that cries too much is often full of eggs inside. If it has loss of appetite, have live shrews given to it; likewise a newborn puppy before it has opened its eyes. If it frequently vomits its food, take scammony to the weight of a quarter of an obol, and as much cumin, and, having ground these, sprinkle their powder on fatty pork, and give it to the bird as food. But if it cannot eat, take ... egg white and put the said powder in it, and put it into its mouth. Likewise, for the same, if it throws up its food, take raw eggs and break them into goat's milk; then have this whole mixture cooked, and give it three times to the hawk to eat, and it will be healed. [The same complete instructions above are repeated a second time, essentially verbatim, in the source manuscript at this point, through the section on vomiting.] [If it begins to molt, free it from all work, and give it food in abundance. For as often as it hungers, it will have that many breaks in its feathers; and in this a secret of nature is noted. Green turf placed beneath its feet is good for it, and the sun's warmth, unless great heat presses in.] If it has fevers, give it juice of wormwood three or four times, and hen's flesh as food; or this: bind its right shin tightly, and in the middle of the leg a vein will appear, and bleed it very carefully. In its leg there are four veins: one in front, another below, another outside, another behind, above the larger claw. You can know whether a bird has a fever if its wings droop and it holds its head lowered, and trembles, and shows as it were cold in its feathers, or takes food reluctantly, or takes it eagerly but digests it poorly. If it is very thirsty, take powder of lovage stalk and dill and fennel reed, and cook these with wine, and mix in a spoonful of honey, and give it the strained liquid to drink, or put it into its mouth, or on one day give it flesh smeared with honey, on the second day flesh smeared with cold rose oil. If it suffers from the gall, sprinkle powder of willow flowers on its food. If its wings droop, take goose blood and fat; rub its wings with the blood in the sun, and give it fatty goose flesh to eat. Likewise, better: take laurel oil and wash its wings with it, and anoint its armpits beneath the wings. Likewise, take pig's gall, and anoint its wings with it, or dip its food in verbena juice; sage juice works the same. If its wings have gout, boil ground ivy in water, and its cooked, well-crushed leaves, and bind them around its wings (along the sides), and soak its food in that same water. Likewise if it has gout in its feet. If moths eat its feathers, let it eat goat's flesh, dipped in vinegar, and rub its wings often with warm vinegar and laurel oil. If you wish to remove a broken feather without pain, take the blood of a rat, or of the small creature called a 'shrew,' and anoint the place of the feather, and it will fall out; and afterward, from honey boiled to a great thickness, make a little rod the shape of the hole where the feather stood, and insert it into the hole, and a new feather will emerge. Likewise anoint its feathers with the warm juice of the poppy herb, and dip its food in the same juice. If it has a broken bone in the leg or wing, bind warm aloe over it, and leave it for a day and a night. Likewise, chicken dung cooked in vinegar, bound over it and left for a day and a night. If the bird is restless on its perch or on the hand of the one carrying it, boil myrrh in water, and sprinkle its body with that water, and dip its food in it, up to nine times. If it suffers the sickness called 'cramp,' let its food be dipped in juice of wormwood. Likewise rub its feet with warm lamb's blood, or with warm wine in which nettles have been boiled; and dip its food in that same wine. If it cannot excrete, give it cock's gall to eat, or boiled white tortoises. If it is too loose, give it a little juice of henbane to drink, or boiled white tortoises. If it has lice, take juice of wormwood or water boiled with wormwood, and, as it sits in the sun, pour this over its feathers and its whole body. If it has nurtured a stone in its belly, give it ointment and butter to eat. For the same, wrap aloe herb and powder of celery in the hearts of small birds and give it to eat; thus you will be able to more conveniently apply any medicine given to birds. Whoever wishes to keep his hawk fat should give it beef or pork, and this from males. Whoever wishes to keep it lean should give it young hens soaked in water. Whoever wishes to keep it in balance should give it old hens. Whoever wishes to have it quick in hunting should give it a good throat-pouch, and shut it in darkness with only a little light, and hunt it on alternate days. If you wish it to catch a hare or rabbit, teach it this in its youth and tie rings on its legs near its feet, a hand's-breadth apart, and it will catch it without injury. Let the wild hawk fast a great deal, and it will grow tame. In its youth let birds be kept neither too hot nor too cold. In the places where they are kept, always have mint and sage growing. Let it perch on willow leaves or on willow or fir wood. From the blood of tender young birds it takes much strength, and boldness and eagerness for hunting. Give it a bath of cold water. Do not handle its wings too much, unless the wings droop unevenly. Finally, lest we seem to have entirely disregarded the sayings of such great authors as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion - accounted among natural histories as most commonly known - we have thought it fitting to insert into this our work these things from the book of noble birds and their medicines. There follows [a chapter] on the bird properly called the 'falcon.'

The falcon is a most noble bird: directed at prey, it flies most impetuously and is less cautious in guarding itself. And so, when the falcon is to be sent after prey, it is held back by its master, and the bird to be caught is not shown to it, until it has first been given some distance, so that it may pursue the prey with a measured onset. In hunting the heron, when two falcons are released together, they fly companionably. One makes for the heights, the other flies low near the ground, namely so that the one striving upward may knock the flying heron down by its impact, and the one flying below may catch it as it falls. There are two kinds of falcons: one ignoble, which catches a bird only through much labor and being reduced by hunger; the other noble, which naturally catches a bird with little effort. The first kind, reckoned baser, when it has driven the heron to the ground and is on the point of catching it, the heron disgorges from its mouth an eel or other fish it had recently swallowed. Without delay the ignoble falcon lets the caught heron fly free into the open air, and, preferring the offered, foul-smelling gift, gladly seizes it more quickly. The noble falcon does not act thus; indeed, scorning the gift cast out by the heron, it presses on more sternly to catch and punish the cunning bird.

The ignoble falcon signifies especially wicked deans and prelates of the church, or secular judges, who, having taken money, release the guilty and, letting crimes go unpunished, in a detestable manner, according to Isaiah, justify the wicked for the sake of gifts.
The falcon, moreover, has in its chest a sharp and hard bone, which nature has provided it for striking its prey.

Griffins are birds, as James [and Pliny] say, which are so exceedingly fierce and of such great body that they overcome and kill armed men in combat. [For they have very large, hooked claws, with which they tear apart men and beasts. The griffin's claws, moreover, are of such capacity that cups fit for human use are made from them.] These guard gold and gems, in Asian Scythia, in a certain inaccessible place, and, because they besiege wealthy visitors, access there is rare, since they tear apart men who are seen, as if created by God to punish the rashness of avarice. The Arimaspians fight with them to seize emerald stones, whose kind is most precious in those same regions.

As is found in the Gloss on the book of Exodus, where the birds forbidden by the Law are distinguished, this bird is four-footed, with a head and wings like an eagle's, though much larger; in the rest of its body it resembles a lion. And it dwells in the Hyperborean mountains, most hostile to horses and to men.
As the Experimentator says, it places an agate stone in its nest, and there is no doubt this is for some remedy. It is established, then, that stones were given by God for some remedy.

The gracocenderon is an eastern bird, said to be endowed with wondrous chastity and temperance. This bird, indeed, among all the living creatures of the earth, completes its reproduction with the least mating. For it mates only once a year, and this for the glory of offspring alone; and for this reason it is free of all lust.

Let man, capable of reason, blush, who mates indiscriminately at every season and has no measure of that temperance, but exhausts his feeble body with lust and does not fear to hasten his days through the excess of his indulgence.

The 'gosturdi' are quite small birds, very similar in color to the earth; they have a small crest of feathers on the head. They fly not in the manner of other birds, but imitate the waves of the sea, which, driven by the wind, now rise high, now sink low. Of these it is commonly reported that a toad broods their eggs, laid on the ground. Once the chicks have hatched from these, the parents then, for the first time, care for them and bring them food, until they can attempt flight.

They signify certain most wicked men placed in the world, who, when they see their sons adorned with good character, not imitators of their own wickedness, at once consider them as if they were strangers; but afterward, if they turn to wickedness, recognize them as their own, and provide the fuel of crimes for their wickedness.

Cranes are birds that fly in orderly formation, like letters. Pliny, Solinus, James, Ambrose, and Isidore describe the crane. As often as they set their course, they go under a kind of military standard. For the one that leads the whole column corrects the others with her voice, so that they do not abandon formation; and when she grows hoarse, another succeeds her in this duty. By night they divide the watches among themselves, so that every tenth one stays sleepless. Those keeping watch hold small stones while standing on one foot raised from the ground, so that, as it falls when they begin to fall asleep, they wake at the sound and cry out. They sleep, moreover, with their head tucked beneath a wing, resting alternately on each foot. The leader, with neck erect, watches and looks ahead. But when they must fly far, they strive for the higher reaches of the sky, so that they may survey, from a loftier vantage point, the lands they seek.

As the Experimentator says, cranes, if they see rain-clouds ahead, cry out and clamor and urge their leader to a swifter flight. When they land on the ground to feed, their leader raises her head high, and this to keep watch over all, while the rest graze securely; but if she sees a man, she cries out, so as to make the unwary alert. Their flesh is heavier than that of other birds, whence it must be that a crane, killed, be kept one day in summer, two in winter, before being eaten, namely so that its flesh becomes more digestible and tender.

Cranes always first gather at the edge of the land, and always oppose the wind as they fly. The crane has a single passage of intestine. About to cross the Black Sea, they swallow sand; they sometimes have a stone in the stomach, which they vomit up. Of this stone, those with experience have said that this same stone, through the mediation of fire, turns into gold. And this is plausible, because it is probable that there are, in many places, certain stones (called 'orichalcum') from which the finest gold is made. And these stones, or ones like them, cranes take up from their places and swallow and vomit up again when they have returned to us. They also burden themselves with small stones to a moderate weight, lest, in the first stages of their journey, they be worn out by excessive lightness. So, raised on high, they seek out the narrow straits, and indeed it is easy for them to judge with their eyes the distance of the journey they must complete. So when they know they have reached the middle of the crossing, they free their feet of the burden of stones. This sailors have often reported, being drenched by a rain of stones falling from that event. They do not vomit up the sand before they have safely reached their resting-place. There is common concern among all of them for the exhausted, so much so that if any fail, all rally together and support the weary ones, until they recover their strength through rest. Their color reveals their age; for they turn black in old age. The Pygmy people are said to fight with them, and to have a truce when the cranes depart. The female crane stands still while trodden by the male in mating. Aristotle speaks of the Pygmies in the book On the Natures of Animals, relating thus: Toward the northern region, beyond Egypt, where the Nile flows, cranes arrive in wintertime, whom the Pygmies, men a cubit tall, meet and fight with.
The Gloss, too, on that passage of Ezekiel: The Pygmy people were in your towers, says that such a people exists in the regions of the East.

But Aristotle himself says thus, that this is indeed not a fiction, but that there is found, in point of fact, a certain small kind of men, and small horses likewise, dwelling in mountainous places. Cranes, moreover, sometimes fly all the way to the ends of the earth, so as to find land suited to their constitution; and they always oppose the wind as they fly. It is said that, flying after winter from the mountains of the East, they swallow golden sands and orichalcum stone, and afterward vomit it up in the lands across the sea. The fighting of cranes is so fierce and persistent that it is possible to catch one by hand [during the fight, so absorbed are they in it].

The 'glutis' is a bird, as Pliny says. It puts out a long tongue, whence it is given its name in Greek. This bird, as winter approaches and the swallows and storks depart, at the start of their migration, flattered by the company of those departing, eagerly sets out on the journey, but afterward, finding the flight laborious, is led to regret it. But since it is loath to return unaccompanied, it follows some birds, yet with such great reluctance and short daily stages that winter overtakes it before its journey is complete. But the 'cicramus,' a bird of Asia, perseveres more hastily and hastens, with untiring effort, to the lands it seeks. It also urges on its companions of the journey more insistently at night, and reminds them of the journey.

These two birds signify any pilgrims, whom we often see marked with the cross, whether to the Holy Land to recover the glorious sepulchre of Christ and the Lord's temple, or in other parts of the world, where the church's need calls its devoted sons. There are, then, among these, many who are pleased by the agreeable company of their neighbors, but who, when they have experienced even a little of the labor of the journey, seek a dispensation. Rome multiplies legates, who, through money, sanctify them and, by letters, commend them, freed from their sins. Good health, and truly blessed indulgence for all sins - and those who have earned it truly rejoice! But oh, how many monks are there in cloisters, who for a long time have endured long fasts, harsh discipline, an almost continual silence, rough clothing, and nightly vigils, and in all this a meager diet and scarcely any comfort: and all this they have endured for very many years, and yet have not yet received letters of any indulgence. I believe you, Paul; and I believe also your successors in the apostolate. I believe, I say, you, who said with a truthful mouth that the Lord will render to each according to his labor. Let me pass over our Friars Preachers, who, worn down by continual studies and vigils, having not money at their belt but rather the parchments of Paul, going about, not on horses or in carriages, but on tired limbs and feet, circle the lands with their preaching. But what should I then say of the Friars Minor, who, girded with a hard cord and without the covering of a cape or cloak, clothed in a tunic over bare skin, walk barefoot upon icy snow as if upon wool - if they did not receive a reward according to their labor? You, then, O pilgrim, marked as the 'glutis' bird, if you have vowed a vow to God by taking the cross: if your strength suffices, fulfill your vow, do not seek a dispensation, unless such necessity presses that you may be excused before the face of Christ himself as judge, who indeed, though persuaded by the Jews and the chief priests to come down from the cross, refused, but remained on the cross even unto death. You, then, imitate Christ; imitate the cicramus, the prudent bird, which joyfully goes ahead, keeps its companions alert, and rouses the sleepy ones.

The cock is a bird crested at the throat and on the head. Cocks know the stars and mark the three-hour divisions of the day by their crowing. They go to roost with the sun and announce the coming day with their crowing. This bird has legs armed with opposing spurs. Hens too sometimes have spurs, but this by an error of nature rather than by its design. When it is about to give its crow, it beats its wings, to make itself more alert. In the depth of night it crows more forcefully, at dawn more lightly. [When it has labored through the night, in the morning it calls the hens to feed.] Its crowing is carried with the wind and heard farther off than can be estimated. And so, with its crowing, it calms horses, rouses camels, and is even said to drive away phantoms. Many herbs that nourish the cock kill other animals. As the Experimentator says, the cock raises its tail and curves it like a half-circle. Its image sits on church towers, and it turns its beak against the wind. When about to sleep, it climbs high and rests on one foot. When it raises its feathers around its neck, shaking itself, it makes itself bolder. The lion fears a white cock. A cock, growing old to decrepit age, produces from itself an egg, from which the basilisk is bred. But in this generation many things must coincide. It lays the egg in warm, abundant dung, and there it is brooded in place of a father. After a long time, then, a chick emerges and grows strong as the chicks of ducks do. Animals of this kind have tails like a snake's, but the rest of the body like a cock's. Those who say they have seen the creation of such an animal say that there is no shell to the egg at all, but it has a very tough and strong skin, so tough that it can withstand the strongest blows. Some are of the opinion that, after the cock has laid the egg, a snake or a toad broods it. But this is doubtful, and we leave it uncertain. We have this much only in the writings of the ancients, that a certain kind of basilisk is bred from an egg which a decrepit, aging cock has laid. The flesh of young cocks is harder to digest, and of less moisture, than that of hens (or capons). But the flesh of decrepit cocks is more tender than that of younger cocks. Capon's flesh has a certain viscosity, but this dissolves in cooking. If several cocks are together in one enclosure of a courtyard, one rules over the rest, having defeated them. The end is often a fight to the death. If a cock ever defeats a rival, it at once crows in victory and proclaims itself the ruler; but the defeated one is hidden away, silent, and bears its servitude with difficulty. The victor, on the contrary, struts proudly with lofty neck, its crest raised high, alone among birds looking to the sky, raising its curved tail on high. And so they are a terror even to lions. And this because it is likened to the basilisk, as some say; or rather - as we believe - a fear of the cock is naturally implanted in the lion. When the hens die, the cock, wasting away with grief, abstains from crowing out of sorrow.

The hen, as Augustine says, is a bird most attentive to her chicks: she gathers them beneath her wings and warms them, and often defends and protects them against kites. Sometimes proud chicks, fleeing her caressing wings, become prey for birds of prey.

Pliny: a certain nettle is deadly to the touch for hens' chicks, which the hen-mothers, naturally recognizing, guard against, and, having seized the root, try to pull up the nettle, but often cannot, and indeed often burst inside their bodies from the very effort.

She breaks up crumbs of bread or grain for them, and calls them with a broken voice. James: eggs are stolen from hens daily, but they do not cease laying eggs for this, if you leave them one (the devil does the same with sins).
Those that exceed the proper measure in laying die quickly. John: but when she has laid eggs in a hidden place, rising and clucking, she betrays them to thieves.
[a near-duplicate passage repeats this same account, attributed to John]

The hen, then, as Pliny says, carries eggs from which males will hatch on the right side of her belly, and eggs from which females will hatch on the left. Those that are rounder at the pointed end produce females; but oblong eggs, sharp at the end, produce a male. Oblong eggs are more pleasant in taste. In all eggs, in the vital center, there is a small drop, as it were, of blood, which they believe is the bird itself, thinking this is produced first, at every stage. This same drop leaps and the creature itself pulses within the egg; from all the rest of the liquid of the egg nothing is incorporated into the chick. Its food is in the yolk. In all of them, before hatching, the head is larger than the whole body, the eyes, pressed together, larger than the head. As the chick grows, however, the white turns to the center, and the yolk spreads around it. On the twentieth day it moves, and the voice of the now-living creature is heard within the shell. From that time it grows feathers, positioned so that it has its head above its right foot, and its right wing over its head. The yolk, meanwhile, gradually diminishes. All birds are born feet first, contrary to all other animals. Some hens lay twin eggs and sometimes hatch twins. In Egypt, by a quite marvelous skill, eggs are brought to completion and chicks hatched without hens brooding them. For men there open up the sand and, taking dung, wrap the eggs in it, and thus, covering them with sand, they are warmed by the heat of the sun and the dung, and so, in due time, they come to completion, and the extracted eggs crack open at the shell and the chicks emerge. We believe the same happens in cold regions, if the eggs are wrapped in warm dung and carefully buried in a great quantity of very hot manure.

As the Experimentator says, there are some hens that always lay twins. It is indeed remarkable in the cock, which, calling the hens, feeds them, and, while feeding them, drives them to the labors of impregnation and childbirth. For, as the Experimentator says, the hen labors greatly in laying; and yet (as the philosopher John says), after laying she sings, and this according to the Gospel: A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, etc. Seeking food, she turns over dust with her feet and so obtains her living.

Brooding hens are more barren of eggs than non-brooding ones. Many hens, and geese, and peacocks lay wind-eggs, that is, eggs without mating. But these are small and tasteless and are moister than others. And if anyone sets one of these to be brooded, its condition will not change, but it will remain white and yellow. When a hen broods in the warm summer, the shells of the eggs crack of themselves, and the chicks emerge sooner than in cold weather. There are certain hens that always produce twins, but one of the twins is small and the other large. And it often happens that the small one is deformed. And the reason is this: because the larger one occupied the space, and the small one lay compressed, and so it happens that its limbs are poorly formed and produce a deformity. In Gaul a chick was seen with two heads and one body; both heads sought food and passed it into the one body. It had four feet, but two hung useless, and it ran on the others. The best brooding is before the spring equinox; those hatched after the solstice do not reach their full proper size, and the later they are hatched, the smaller they remain.

The egg first emerges from the wider end, then from the pointed end. The pointed part of the egg contains the head, the rounder part the hindquarters of the chick. Pliny is the authority that a hen, on the day she has laid an egg, does not die from the bite of an asp - indeed, it is a medicine for those bitten. For this reason, something good, even if very small, should always be done daily for Christ, so that on that occasion one may be protected from the impending harm of the devil. It is most useful to brood eggs laid within ten days; older or too fresh eggs are infertile. They should be set in odd numbers. On the fourth day after brooding begins, if, held up to the light with the point of the egg toward the hand, a pure and uniform color shines through, they are judged sterile; others should be substituted for these. There is also a test in water: an empty egg, thrown into water, floats, but a full one sinks and should be set to brood. They forbid shaking them as a test, since eggs whose vital veins have been disturbed do not hatch. Brooding begins after the new moon, because those begun earlier often fail. They hatch more quickly in warm weather, whence in summer they produce chicks on the nineteenth day, but in winter on the twenty-ninth. If it thunders suddenly, they often fail; and, hearing the hawk's voice, they are also spoiled. The remedy against thunder is an iron nail placed crosswise among the eggs, or earth placed upright.
Aristotle: cocks are said to abstain from crowing when the hens have died.

Pliny: the good breeding of hens is shown by a red comb. Catarrh is most hostile to hens; this occurs especially between harvest-time and vintage-time. The remedy is a feather inserted crosswise through the nostrils and moved about every day, or garlic as food. Pliny is the authority that if you melt gold and mix in the limbs of hens, they consume the gold within themselves, so that it can be said that gold is poison to hens. [The yolk of an egg laid at the full moon removes every stain from a woolen garment, if you rub it well with the yolk and afterward wash it. The egg, however, should be cooked soft in the middle.]

The capon is a bird, as the Book of Properties says, deprived of its testicles, which Scripture calls 'pepo'; but we commonly call it 'capon.' They are said to fatten more quickly, since they are kept from lust.

As the Experimentator says, the capon fattens among the hens, but never fertilizes them by impregnating them; it feeds with them, but never defends them. It does not crow to mark the hours of day or night. These are useful for nothing but the kitchen. For their flesh is stronger than that of all winged creatures: for it generates good blood and excellent nourishment.

bibl.author: Sermones Iordani de Saxonia Iordanus de Saxonia

cit.quote: Jordan, master of the Order of Preaching Friars, said in a certain sermon - he was speaking, indeed, to canons and clergy in a synod: Shebna the scribe, he says, shall be carried away like a capon, and to where? To no other place, indeed, than the devil's kitchen. And why? Because he does not breed and does not crow. He does not beget spiritual sons, and would that he did not beget carnal ones either! He does not crow, as he is bound sevenfold to give praise in the day, according to the canonical and appointed hours of day and night. And so, useful for nothing else, not only Shebna but everyone who, without due fruit, professes himself a cleric or a canon, will be carried off to hell, to the devil's kitchen.

James and the Lapidary: they are sometimes castrated after living three years, and afterward allowed to live five or six years more; and so in its liver a precious stone is found, called the 'alectorius.' Once it has conceived this stone in its liver, then, it never afterward drinks. Whence if anyone holds this stone in his mouth, it quenches thirst.

Sometimes the feathers of this bird's chest are plucked and burned smooth with nettles, so that orphaned chicks may be placed under it in place of their mother, and it warms them by the heat that its bared body gives the chicks. Thus, once it has found relief from the cold and a remedy through the burning of the nettles in the placement of the chicks beneath it, conceiving a maternal affection, it warms them, and feeds them in its mother's place, and forms sounds after the manner of hens, so as to call, with a broken voice, those wandering off.

div.head: 60. De gallo silvestri qui et ‘phasianus’ dicitur

cit.quote: The wild cock, also called 'phasianus' by Pliny, is fittingly given a name related to Gaul's own [gallus]. It is a very beautiful bird, with shimmering feathers, splendid like fire, sometimes sky-blue and green, with a red brilliance interwoven with the feathers. It seems to have two ears on its head, with feathers standing up, which it raises and lowers at will. It lacks a crest on its head and spurs on its legs. Yet, despite lacking these weapons, it is known to be a spirited and bold bird. Fowlers, knowing this, make a shield from white linen cloth, in the middle of which they place a small red patch. The cock, gazing intently at this redness against the white, fixes its eye and marvels at the unfamiliar sight. Without delay the fowler, seeing it transfixed by the sight, forces it, by the effort of the shield, to retreat backward, until he drives the captive bird into nets set up at a distance. And this is the hunting of the wild cock.

It signifies those who, led by curiosity of sight, are gradually caught in the devil's nets, and who, while less on guard against what is to come, delighted by curiosity for present things, fall even into the act of sin, from which vanities they were unwilling to turn their eyes away. It can also signify those who, while wishing to direct the eyes of the mind toward spiritual contemplation, grasp at certain fantasies with a hungry imagination and, while they believe they see God, or his angels, spirits of light, are deluded in many ways by the spirit of error and darkness.

As the Experimentator says, the wild cock (or, as Pliny calls it, the 'pheasant'), fixing its beak in the ground, hides its head, and thus believes itself entirely hidden. In rainy weather it grows sad, and then hides in the brambles and woods. Around evening or dawn it comes out of the woods, and then it is easily hunted. (It sheds its feathers because of its fatness, and renews itself again.) Its flesh is finer and lighter than that of other wild birds, except for the chicks of partridges.

The jay, as Isidore says, is named from its chattering. For it is the most talkative kind of bird, and troublesome with its cries. It moves from one topic to another, chattering, nor can anyone hardly pass by it without being chattered at. It is said to imitate the voices or melodies of other birds not for the delight of joy, but for chattering's sake.

This bird, caught in its youth, is caged, so that it may be taught to speak articulate words, and, once it escapes, it is all the more eager to chatter. It sometimes happens, however, that, while not watching out for itself and intent on its chattering, the sparrowhawk suddenly seizes it. This bird is marked with such variety of feathers that no color of any other bird is said to be lacking to it. It is often said to go mad, so much so that the Experimentator says that, out of excessive fury, it hangs itself, raving, among the forked branches of a tree.

The jackdaw is a bird which some falsely think is the same bird as the jay. There is much difference between them, since the jay is marked with varied colors in its feathers, while the jackdaw is a bird of a single color, black over its whole body: for it is of the crow kind, though smaller in body. It gladly nests in the tall trees of forests, and this in such numbers that often seven pairs of jackdaws build their nests in a single tree. For these birds get along remarkably well with one another. It is an exceedingly noisy bird, especially at mating time, and when the spring season stirs mating, the male, for love's sake, feeds the female. The flesh of its young is edible, especially if skinned.

The ibis is a bird, as Solinus says, dwelling around the banks of the river Nile, which devastates serpents' eggs and, from these, brings a most pleasing food to its young: thus the increase of harmful offspring is made rare. Nor do these birds benefit only the borders of Egypt. For when winged serpents from Arabia wish to fly over, before they cross the borders, the ibis birds, roused, go out in force and meet the pestilent swarms in the air, and there devour the whole army of serpents. The venom of these serpents is so quick that death follows the bite before the pain does. This bird conceives through the mouth. If anyone eats its eggs, he dies.
This bird cleanses itself with its beak, pouring water over its rear parts.

But when it becomes constipated from too much food, as Pliny and Solinus say, resting over the Nile, it draws out indigestible food from its secret parts with its beak. And in this it signifies slanderers, who are always ready to spread what they have heard about their neighbors and to interpret doubtful matters for the worse. Around the shores of the sea, or of a river, or of ponds, this bird walks by night and by day, seeking either dead little fish or some carcass that has been cast up, already putrid or decayed, from the waters. Yet it never enters the water, but delights only in the carcasses cast ashore. Pelusium has black ibis birds, but the rest of the country has white ones.

Some say this bird is the stork; but if this is true, it is strange why the authors have set differences between storks and ibis birds. Those plainly lie who say the ibis birds are the same as storks, unless perhaps they mean a kind of stork not usually seen in our part of the world, Europe, since Pliny says of the ibis that it has a hooked beak, which is certainly false of storks, which have a long, straight beak, sharp at the tip, and not hooked.

bibl.author: Antiquitates Iudaice Flavii Iosephi Flavius Iosephus

cit.quote: Josephus: it is found in the Histories of Josephus that Moses, while still young, sent against the Ethiopians by the king of Egypt, took ibis birds and made them go ahead of the army through an inaccessible desert, so that serpents might be put to flight by fear of them. The Ethiopians, however, could in no way have suspected that this desert could be made passable for Moses because of the serpents. Whence it happened that Moses found Ethiopia unguarded on the desert side, and, attacking unexpectedly, subjected the whole nation to servitude and took their queen as his wife.

The 'iboz' is a bird of the East. It is a spirited and very strong bird. There is a perpetual hatred between this bird and the horse kind; and this is the reason: the iboz is a bird that grazes on grasses, like a goose. It has, moreover, a horrible voice, which, in a certain way, with its neighing, imitates the voice of a horse; but this is most grievous to hear. The horse hates the iboz bird, because it is terrified by its voice. The iboz, in turn, hates the horse, because it drives it from its pastures. When, then, the iboz bird grazes on grasses, the horse, driven by envious zeal, drives it away. But when the iboz sees the horse standing secure at pasture, it lets out its horrible cry and terrifies the horse and forces it to flee, and thus, having driven it off, sometimes kills it through the horse's excessive agitation.

The 'incendula' is a bird of the East, said to be of the raven's kind; this bird is cunning and very spirited: it fights with the eagle-owl. And since the eagle-owl has weak sight at midday, the incendula bird comes and, fighting more forcefully and winning, eats the eagle-owl's eggs. But when the tables are turned, the eagle-owl, seeing more clearly by night, fights with the incendula bird in the silence of the deep night, and, since the incendula cannot see at night, the eagle-owl instead, by victory, plunders its eggs, and thus repays evil for evil.
The swallow, as the Book of Properties says, is a most agile bird, with a small beak, pleasing form, and a most fitting blackness. It is white on the belly, reddish beneath the throat.

As the Experimentator says, it has black flesh, many feathers and large wings, and therefore has a swift flight. It announces the day (singing before dawn) and rouses sleepers (and invites them to praise of the Creator). Its blood, drawn from beneath the right wing, heals the eyes. It has a forked tail.

It flies in winding curves and through twisting circuits. It is chattering. It catches its food in flight. Solinus: it has a certain foreknowledge, in that it abandons a roof about to fall and does not seek out ridge-tops. It is most skillful in building nests and raising its young. There are some that carry gems in their liver, as the Book of Properties says. This gem is sometimes found red, sometimes black, and is called 'celidonius': it is beneficial to lunatics and drives away harmful humors; washed in water, it heals sick eyes.

These swallow chicks that have this stone are known by this sign: if, as a sign of peace, they sit in the nest turned mouth to mouth. For the other chicks that do not have it sit turned away from each other.

A swallow, eaten, extinguishes holy fire and cures epileptics. If you roast its chicks in a clay-sealed pot, once the pot is broken you will find two chicks as if kissing each other. If you burn these, their ash, drunk, is effective for reconciling spouses.
[a fragmentary attribution:] of the swallow
Pliny: swallow chicks are at first blind. The females conceive by imagination of desire, or by dust.

Isidore: it is not attacked by other birds, nor is it ever prey. It keeps to the seasons of its coming; it knows when to come and when to return; its arrival announces the beginning of spring. When their chicks' eyes are troubled, the mothers apply celandine as a medicine.

Pliny: this alone, among birds without claws, lives on flesh. In winter they seek out the sunny recesses of mountains, and there are found bare and featherless. They are said not to enter the houses of Thebes.

This bird, lacking everything, builds nests more precious than gold, as Ambrose says, because it builds so wisely. For the nest of wisdom is more precious than gold. For what is wiser than that it should enjoy the freedom of flight and yet warm its little ones in the dwellings of men, so that no one may attack its offspring? Then there is that remarkable thing, by what skill it builds its nests without any helper, as if by mastery of an art; it gathers straws with its beak, and smears them with mud, so as to glue them together. But since it cannot carry mud with its feet, it dips the tips of its feathers in water, so that dust may easily cling to them and become mud, with which it glues the straws together, and in this way builds the whole structure of the nest.

Swallows, then, build their nests with mud, strengthen them with hay, and line them with soft feathers and down, namely for the warming of the eggs, so that the nest is not hard for the young. In feeding their young, they alternate food with the greatest fairness, and with remarkable cleanliness remove the chicks' droppings, and teach the older ones to turn around and expel their waste outside. Swallows lay eggs twice, but the first eggs are often spoiled because of winter. If anyone blinds swallow chicks, their eyes are restored again, as Aristotle says.
But the philosopher Aldhelm says the same thing.

Swallows, as Pliny says, are untrainable, and so are mice, whereas lions and elephants can be tamed and domesticated. There is also another, very small kind of them. These, in the regions of the East, build their nests for themselves from dry moss, so perfectly rounded that the entrance can scarcely be found. In Egypt, then, in a marshy place, where the Nile has been known to overflow its banks, by the continuous joining of their nests they form what is, as it were, an impregnable wall over a stretch of nearly a stadium's length, which could not be accomplished by human labor. They reinforce that marvelous work with straw and chaff. They labor so diligently at this work that it is known that many of them die in the process.

The wagtail, or 'cropa,' is a bird, as the Book of Kyranides says, of an ash-grey color, or sometimes black, or varied. It always shakes its tail while sitting over little streams, whence it is also named 'tremble-tail.'

It signifies those who, subject to a wandering and unstable disposition, nonetheless, trembling in conscience, dread the memory of death, and this when they contemplate the fleeting course of the human condition. Whence David: What man is there who shall not see death?
And in the Second Book of Kings it is said: We all die, and, like water, we glide away.

We call the 'isida' bird so from the sound of its voice. It is indeed a small bird, but most brilliant in the beauty of its feathers. On its back it has a color between green and sky-blue, so beautiful that, if illuminated by the sun's rays from opposite, you will see a sapphire-like sheen in its feathers. But the color on its chest presents the image of burning coals. It has only two toes on its foot, hooked claws, but a small and straight beak. It lives on little fish and stays constantly near waters. With its beak it hollows out caves in the earth, where it gathers its nest and rears its young. Of this bird the common people say - though whether truly or falsely I do not know - that if you strip the skin, with its feathers, from the dead bird and fix the stripped skin to a wall, every year the skin will change its feathers, as if it were still in the body.

It signifies those who, living, have refused to abandon their character and old evil habits, whom death will indeed change, since, in place of delights, they will obtain punishment, in place of vain joy, sorrow, and in place of transient evils, everlasting hell.

[The 'kyliodromos'] is a bird in India which, as soon as it is born, flies toward the sun in the east, and turns with the sun toward the west. It lives only a year and a half, and in that time bears two chicks, a male and a female. Its flesh, eaten, protects a man against epilepsy and many other illnesses.

The 'kym' is a large bird, as Aristotle says, which lives on prey. It has good breeding habits and good character, and is very patient toward hostile birds. It is of great care, and diligently feeds and nourishes its chicks, and not only its own, but also the chicks of a certain most wicked kind of eagle, which drives out its chicks before their time, weary of raising them.

The 'karkolaz' is a bird of the East, naturally cunning and malicious. As Aristotle says, this bird, loving idleness and given to aimless curiosity, is also lazy about producing offspring of its own kind; but since it cannot entirely deny nature's due, when the female has received seed from the male and senses the eggs ripe for laying, she seeks out a wood-pigeon's nest. Thus the deceived pigeon broods eggs of a foreign kind.

The 'komor' is a bird of Arabia, as Aristotle says, and is the best breeder among all kinds of wild birds. For it lays eggs and produces chicks five or six times a year, and no wild bird does this except this one. Birds that live in houses, however, like doves or hens, lay more often. In the komor bird, then, this is considered quite marvelous, that it does not easily lay before certain stars appear in the firmament, which are hidden for a time in between; and the appearance of these stars grants this bird the power of fertility.

The 'kyches' is a bird, as Aristotle says, which cries out with various voices and changes its voice on almost every day. It nests in trees, of wool and hair, and lays its eggs there. When the acorns are ripe, it gathers sufficient food for itself from them. But once the chicks are raised and grown strong for flight, they feed their parents in old age and make them stay in the nests without any labor.

The gull is a bird, as the Gloss says, endowed with a double nature. For, as the Gloss says, on the passage where the unclean birds are forbidden in the Law, this bird dwells both in water and on land, and delights in both elements: swimming in the waters, flying in the air.

'Lucidian' birds are birds, as the Book of Properties and Solinus say, so called as if 'giving light,' whose feathers glimmer in the darkness of night. Whence it happens that those who have the feathers of these birds, when they wish, having cast the feathers ahead into the darkness, direct their paths by the light of these luminous feathers.
This bird is found in the Hercynian forest of Germany, as Pliny says.

The nightingale is a bird of which the blessed Ambrose relates, in the Hexameron, that this ever-watchful guardian, while she warms her eggs in a certain fold and lap of her body, comforts the sleepless labor of the long night with the sweetness of her song. And, as it seems to the blessed Ambrose himself, this bird's chief purpose is that she may, with sweet melodies no less than with the warmth of her body, animate, in their warming, the eggs she broods.
This is indeed astonishing and quite marvelous even in the lion, but not at all to be doubted, since the blessed Augustine and many others have related this same, quite similar thing of the lion.

The 'linachos' is a bird, as Aristotle says, of very sharp sight, and it forces its young to gaze at the sun before their wings are fully grown; and for this it strikes them and turns them toward the sun's disc; and if anyone's eye waters, it kills that one and feeds the others. This bird stays near the sea and feeds on the birds that are in the sea. Sometimes, raised in the air, it looks down at those swimming in the sea below. Then the birds, seeing it, plunge into the sea, terrified with fear. Then the linachos bird descends near the water and forces the birds into so fatal a plunge that they are forced to drown in the water. Then, drowned in the water, the birds are carried by their feathers to the surface of the water, and it seizes these and carries them to land.

The 'lagepus' [hare-foot bird] is a bird, as Pliny says, that has feet like a hare's and down similar to fur; whence it also gets its name. In other respects they are white on the belly, the size of doves. They do not easily feed outside the earth, but, having sought food, return like plunderers to their burrows, and thus live in hiding off their spoils. This bird never grows tame in life, but its body, once killed or dead of natural causes, decays most quickly, and this perhaps because it lived constantly in decaying earth.

There is a certain kind of this bird that is nearly the size of an eagle, laden with feathers. It has a huge head and feathers arranged on its forehead like horns, so that it can be a horror to those who see it. It has very large eyes, blazing like fire; it never closes these, but covers them with a kind of membrane in sleep. It has legs and feet hairy like a hare's, and hooked claws like an eagle's. It lives on prey. It catches and eats hares by night. It cries out at night like the eagle-owl, whence some have said it is of the eagle-owl's kind. It is customary for other birds to be caught most effectively by means of these birds. Some have said this bird can be tamed, and this if you train a chick from the nest.

The kite is a bird, as Isidore says, nearly the size of an eagle. It has claws, feet, and a hooked beak like a hawk's, but its wings are curved and not straight like a hawk's. Yet, weak in strength, it is most rapacious in flight and lies in wait for domestic chicks. It hovers around slaughterhouses and around carcasses.

Pliny: they are thought to have taught the art of steering by the turns of their tail, nature showing in the sky what would be needed in the deep. They are said, indeed, to be afflicted with gout at the time of the solstices. Pliny praised the kite's liver as medicinal.
As the Experimentator says, the kite is bold against small creatures, timid against large ones. It is put to flight by the sparrowhawk, though it is three times its size.

The kite knew its season in the sky; the turtledove and the swallow have their time of departure. For kites among us always stay, both winter and summer. But this is certainly not so among the people of Jerusalem. For the kite around Jerusalem cannot shed its feathers unless it drinks the salt waters of the sea, toward the southern region. Whence, when the time of its molting approaches, leaving the land of its usual habitation, it seeks the southern region.
The 'magnales,' as Aristotle says, are large eastern birds like vultures, red in color, black in feet and beak. They do no harm to men, but only eat the fish they draw out of the river.

The 'melancoriphus' is a bird, as Pliny says, which, though small, is preferred over large winged creatures in fecundity; it lays more than twenty eggs, always in an odd number. It is a most diligent bird toward its chicks, and its diligence is noted in the fact that, though it alone feeds so many chicks, yet when they grow up, so as to be food for birds of prey, they are found very fat. The chicks, once raised from the nest, follow their mother in flocks, and she does not ignore their pleading hunger, until they are able to live by their own effort.

The 'morplex' is a bird so named because it 'strikes with death' [morte plectat]. For it is a swift bird, large as a kite, black as a blackbird, with large claws and a strong beak, plunging into the water like a diving bird, and this because it draws eels and large fish from the bottom of the waters and eats them. This bird builds its nest in the tallest trees and nourishes its chicks there, in a place of great abundance of fish. But when its chicks have grown strong enough to fly, then, as if by a natural instinct, sensing the inconvenient weight, they vomit up the food they had devoured, lest, weighed down by too great a burden of food, they be unable to fly if flight is needed, and be caught by their enemies. Those who have proven this remedy, naturally implanted for their safety, have avoided dangers; but those who have not, have perished. [There is a certain kind of these that is of a very hot nature, so that they catch the air in winter with outstretched wings, and their dung dries out the green trees on which they often rest.]

The Mennonid birds are Egyptian birds, named from the place where Mennon perished, as Isidore and Pliny say. For they are said to fly in flocks from Egypt to Ilium, near the tomb of Mennon, and for this reason the people of Ilium call them the Mennonides. In the fifth year they come to Ilium, and, having circled around for two days, on the third day they enter into battle and tear one another apart in turn with claws and beaks.

The 'meauca' are seabirds, larger than ducks, as the Book of Properties says. They are of an ash-grey color, have short legs, a short neck, grey-blue eyes, a beak saffron-colored in part and red in part. This bird is so named from the sound of its voice: for the meauca always cries out. It is most greedy for corpses, and this human corpses. When a storm is imminent, they cry out most and, as it were, rejoice then, at the approach of a feast of corpses: it seeks the eye in a corpse first. They lie in wait for small animals, wherever they are gathered.

'Merillions' are birds, as the Book of Properties says, commonly so named. For they are not much larger in form or different in color from blackbirds, except that they have different feet, claws, and beak. They are birds eager for prey and, being small and of little strength, are pursuers of small birds. For they fly sociably, like gerfalcons or hawks, and four of them together can catch a swan in this way: the first of them attacks the swan's head, the second and third the wings on either side, and the fourth attacks the chest or neck, and so the burdened swan, surrounded and hemmed in, unable to move, is overcome and caught by the fowler and killed.

Flycatchers are birds taking their name from the fact itself. This bird alone has such a wide-open mouth that no other bird can be compared to it. And in this provident nature is to be praised, which chose to make up, in the gape of its mouth, for what was lacking in speed because of its sluggish flight, for the catching of prey. For it can catch flies and gnats, on which alone it feeds, more easily this way than if it were very swift with a narrow mouth. Though it has a very wide gape, its beak, in proportion to its body, is nevertheless among the smallest of birds. Likewise it has very small feet. Yet it is larger than the turtledove and the dove. Its feet and beak, however, are like the swallow's. It has feathers like the lanner falcon.

The bee-eater is a bird, as Pliny says, which, abounding in natural heat, digs burrows in the ground six feet deep; in these burrows it builds its nest, lays eggs, rears its chicks, and feeds and nourishes them, hidden in the earth, until they reach their due strength. This bird has a sky-blue color on its back, a somewhat reddish chest, and a pale belly.

The blackbird, as James says, was in antiquity called 'medula,' because it makes melody [moduletur]. It gives forth wondrous modes of voice, especially when it perceives that spring is approaching; for in wintertime it is silent, mute. There was a blackbird which, taught by human art, sang nine notes in order according to musical form so perfectly that no musician, with equal harmony, could in any way imitate it. This was, at that time, a wonder and remarkable marvel among the clergy: that a bird, not by the dictate of nature but only by human art, had learned perfect music in nine notes, and, having nearly forgotten its natural song, repeated this alone, often, to the wonder of the rejoicing and admiring crowd.

As the Experimentator says, a domesticated blackbird, against its own nature, eats meat, and from this sings more sweetly. In winter, because of its fat, it can scarcely fly. It gladly bathes itself and cleans its feathers with its beak. Though it is black and unattractive, because of the pleasantness of its voice it moves the mind to affection for itself.

The blackbird, like other birds, does not shed its feathers, as Pliny says. Some say it is called 'merula' because it flies alone, that is, 'mera.' It has a somewhat saffron color on its chest; but blackness occupies the rest of the body. Though it is black everywhere, in Achaea it is white.

Blackbirds, wood-pigeons, and partridges purge their annual distaste [for food] with laurel leaf. The blackbird turns from black to reddish, sings in summer, stammers in winter. It changes its beak to white every year. There is also another kind of them, but much larger: these, called 'goatsuckers' from the fact itself, enter shepherds' stables and fly to the udders of goats for the milk's sake, by which injury the goat's udder withers away and blindness arises in the goats. These birds are sometimes said to lack sight.
The jackdaw, as James says, is named as if 'taking coin' or 'loving coin.' For if it finds gold or silver, it steals it and hides it.

This bird is black, but somewhat handsome and pleasing. It imitates human voices quite perfectly, when trained as a chick. It is said to learn most eagerly and retain most tenaciously in the morning, at sunrise. As the Experimentator says, jackdaw's flesh excites an itching of the head; whence the bird itself desires to be scratched on the head.

The merganser is a bird, as Isidore says, swimming in rivers and ponds. It pursues fish. It is named from 'diving' [mergendo], because it plunges itself into the water. It cannot, however, stay under water very long, since it must recover its breath in the upper air.
[Book of Properties:] the chicks, as soon as they leave the egg, are so vigorous that, should they happen to lose their mother, they can live by their own strength.

Sulpicius Severus: [there is a certain species of these called, from the fact, 'horned,' because they have red feathers on the head like horns. Contrary to every other kind of bird, they have their feet at the tail, so that, when they stand on land, they are upright like a man in bearing.] The blessed Martin, bishop of Tours, by divine power, compelled these birds to abandon the waters, against their nature, and seek out dry and deserted places.

Ambrose relates of these that they often gather signs of the weather; foreseeing a coming storm, they fly back from the middle of the open water and hasten, crying out, toward the safety of the shores.

When the merganser must be struck, it plunges into the water; and this signifies those who make excuses for themselves when they are accused in confession. As the Experimentator says, in winter they are fatter because of the scarcity of movement. For every animal delights in clear weather and wanders more in it than in stormy weather.

The sparrowhawk is a noble bird, as the Book of Properties says, smaller both in form and strength than the gerfalcon. Yet both have the same feather color, and still they refuse to fly together. For it is said to be moved by envy and pride, and when it attacks, it alone wishes to have the honor of victory. This can indeed be supposed, and perhaps rightly. But in truth it is more credible that it simply craves prey alone, lest, having a companion in flight, it must share a companion at the feeding.

Nor is it in doubt that the sparrowhawk disdains its own kind and pursues it as if it were a bird of another kind, and this contrary to the nature of every other kind of bird, since, as Aristotle says, every bird catching prey in flight spares birds of its own kind. The sparrowhawk alone, then, is without this nobility, and in this it resembles man himself, since, among the quadruped animals, man does not cease to lie in wait for an animal of his own kind. [The sparrowhawk, in winter, holds a caught bird alive under its feet all night, because of the cold, and, mindful, as the common people have taught, of the benefit rendered, lets its captive fly free in the morning: a memorable and truly pious example. A sparrowhawk that nests among brambles and in a low place is reckoned excellent; but one that builds its nest high and in tall trees is judged less bold and baser.]

The night-heron is called, as Aldhelm says, the 'raven of night.' It is indeed the bird we call the 'owl.' It loves the darkness of night, but cannot bear to see the sun: for it is a light-fleeing creature. With its grey-blue pupils it does not feel the horror of the darkness of nighttime shadows; but the darker the night is, the more freely, contrary to other birds' sight, it carries on its flight unimpeded. But when day rises, and the sun's brightness spreads around, its sight grows dull, as if it wandered in a kind of darkness. By night it seeks its food, which, if it flew by day, would be attacked by the other birds of the air. The owl, as the common people suppose, seems to foretell men's deaths with its ominous cries. And it signifies those who trust in vain hope in another's death. It delights in human excrement. It pursues mice and every kind of them. It gladly dwells in houses or walls, and there warms its young. It has a huge head, not shaped like other birds. It has a hooked beak like the sparrowhawk's, and the claws of its feet hooked and rough.

The owl is a clever fighter against birds. For, surrounded by a greater number of them, lying on its back, it fights against them with its feet, says Pliny. When attacked by man or by birds, lying on its back, it defends itself with its beak and the claws of its feet. The hawk, however, helps it, by a certain fellowship of nature, and shares in the battle. On the island of Crete, if an owl is ever brought there, it dies at once. Owl's flesh helps paralytics.

The 'nepa' is a bird [and is called in French 'orbegelina,' as if 'hen of darkness,' taking its name from the fact itself]. It is the size of a partridge, and has a long beak, which, driven deep into the earth, seeks the food of worms; and when it sometimes cannot easily free itself, its beak driven deep into the earth, it applies its feet and, by their effort, clears away the dirt in which its open beak had stuck, freeing itself, and rises into the open air. This bird rests by day in hidden places, but flies through the air at evening and at earliest dawn, whence it is hunted at these same hours, and this by broad nets suspended aloft, close to the ground, which, when a catch falls into them, are suddenly released by ropes. [It has a color on its back like the partridge's, and on the chest like the sparrowhawk's.] [This bird is said not to live in England.] [In certain regions it is said not to live.] The nepa has a head pierced through nearly from ear to ear, so that this can readily be verified by the eyes. It places its ear to the ground and clearly hears the worm gnawing.

The pelican [onocrotalus] is a bird with a long beak, dwelling in the regions of the East. When it wishes to utter its voice, it puts its head in the water and thus lets out a cry like a bellow. As the Experimentator says, not without a reason of nature does this bird have certain little pouches in its throat, in which it first places its food and, after a while, sends what it has received into a second stomach. For it has only two stomachs, one of which is in the throat, and in the other it cooks and digests its food; this is not so in other birds.
This bird has a long beak. There are two kinds of them: one aquatic, the other of the wilderness. This alone among birds lacks a spleen, as Aristotle says.
Isidore says that this bird stores much food at once in its belly.

And in this it signifies the miserly, of whom it is said: The riches he swallowed he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them out of his belly. Afterward, however - when hungry - it draws it out and eats it again.
Defiled by this uncleanness, it is forbidden in the Law.

Physicians say that, by the example of this bird, Hippocrates learned the remedy of the enema. For as Hippocrates walked along the seashore, he saw a pelican distressed, constipated by an excess of food. And when, running here and there, it could not relieve itself, drawing salt seawater with its beak, it injected it into its rear with its beak, and soon, by this natural remedy, was relieved with effect.
The bird, then, as Pliny says, is rapacious and lives on prey; in spring it purges its bowels, and this after the manner of a ruminant.

The 'otho' [long-eared owl] is a bird smaller than the eagle-owl, larger than owls, as Pliny says. This bird is commonly called 'huans' from the sound of its voice. It seems to have ears, from its prominent feathers. It has a hooked beak and feet. It hunts mice, lives on prey, and feeds on flesh; the other birds hold it in hatred. By night it cries horribly 'hoo, hoo,' improperly resembling a human voice, so that you would think a man contracted with cold was crying out. This bird has particular lands where it gives forth these cries; but there are many lands where they are silent and do not cry out.

The 'osma' is a bird as large as a swan: it dwells in river waters and fishponds. It has a large and strong beak. They are eager for fish as prey, which they pierce through the body with their beak, and it seems that nature gave them an instrument suited to receiving food fit for so great a body. For they have, as it were, a sack-like receptacle, wide and long, from the throat itself down to the chest, in which they store a great quantity of fish at once. And see how fittingly: so that nature need not be in want, spread over so great a mass, but, the food gradually digested within the belly, finds ready what it can offer as nourishment. Birds of this kind are found nowhere in numbers, except wherever the water is more widespread and there is a great abundance of fish. For they very quickly empty even a great quantity of fish from a small water with their gluttony.

div.head: 97. De oriolis quod est genus pico martii

cit.quote: Orioles are birds, as the Book of Properties says, so commonly named from the sound of their voice. They are golden in color throughout, except that on the wings they have certain feathers marked with a sky-blue variety.

Pliny: they hang their nest from the tiniest branches of trees with wondrous delicacy, so that, if you saw the nest placed on the ground, you would think it hanging in the air alone. [And this because it cannot bear the stench of its own dung, and, if long troubled by its own dung, dies.] They roof the nest against rain and protect it with dense foliage. These are said to be of the woodpecker kind, though smaller.

The pelican is so called (as if) having 'grey skin' [pellem canam]. Whence, Augustine and Isidore say, it has grey feathers. This bird dwells in Egypt; it is most abundant around the Nile. Loving its chicks, when they finally become troublesome to it, it kills them, and, mourning them for three days, striking its own side with its beak, revives them with its own blood.

It is said, moreover, that they do this same thing when they find their chicks killed by a serpent that had lain in wait for them. The Experimentator says of this bird that, after the shedding of its blood, the pelican is so weakened that, unable to leave the nest, its chicks are forced to leave the nest for its feeding and their own. But some of the chicks, sluggish through cowardice, are unwilling to leave to feed either themselves or their mother, and perish. Others, however, leave and feed their mother. Still others are worse, who indeed feed themselves, but utterly neglect their mother. And when the mother, after her recovery, sees this, she nourishes the devoted children, but casts out and despises the undutiful ones. There are two kinds of pelicans. One is aquatic, which lives on fish; the other dwells on land and feeds on serpents.
